abstract:
  "The Diffusion Decision Model (DDM) decomposes response time and accuracy data from speeded decision-making tasks into cognitive process parameters. DDM analyses still often fit each participant separately and test point estimates afterwards, which discards uncertainty, partly because hierarchical estimation is hard to specify and slow to run. The bmm R package implements one-step Bayesian hierarchical estimation of DDM parameters through three approaches: the EZ-Diffusion Model, which works from summary statistics and fits in minutes; the Censored-Shifted Wald; and full DDM likelihood estimation via the Wiener first-passage time distribution. This tutorial centers on the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model as a primary analysis of condition effects on drift, boundary separation, non-decision time, and the starting point. Three tutorials apply the approaches to the classic lexical decision dataset of Wagenmakers et al. (2008). On these data, the two condition effects tested across approaches, emphasis on boundary separation and word frequency on drift, agreed in sign, rank order, and evidence category between the EZ-Diffusion Model and the full DDM at a fraction of the computational cost; the absolute values of boundary separation and non-decision time differed. The comparison illustrates the case on one dataset rather than settling it. A parameter recovery study shows that the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model recovers a biased starting point, and the tutorial introduces the preprocessing tools bmm provides for contaminant responses. After working through the tutorials, readers will be able to preprocess RT data, fit the EZ-Diffusion Model as a primary analysis, and decide when a trial-level approach is needed."

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| eval: true
pacman::p_load(here, bmm, brms, rtdists, tidyverse, tidybayes, patchwork)
source(here("functions", "clean_plot.R"))

# --- Helpers -----------------------------------------------------------------

# Format estimate with 95% CrI
fmt_est <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  sprintf("%.*f [%.*f, %.*f]", digits, x["Estimate"],
          digits, x["Q2.5"], digits, x["Q97.5"])
}
# Wall-clock of the slowest chain (chains run in parallel): the statistic the
# text reports as fitting time. Read from the archived fit, never typed.
fit_secs  <- function(fit) max(rowSums(rstan::get_elapsed_time(fit$fit)))
fit_time  <- function(fit) {
  s <- fit_secs(fit)
  if (s < 90) sprintf("%.0f s", s)
  else if (s < 3600) sprintf("%.1f min", s / 60)
  else sprintf("%.1f h", s / 3600)
}
# Bayes Factors: format (with infinity) and the verbal label the text uses
# (thresholds of 3, 10, 100 after @kass1995bayes, as introduced in Tutorial 1)
# Savage-Dickey ratios are density estimates from the posterior draws, and very
# large values are imprecise (Oberauer et al., 2026): anything at or above
# 10,000, including an underflow to infinity, prints as "$\geq$ 10,000". The
# helper returns the operator too, so prose writes "BF `r bf_fmt(x)`".
bf_fmt <- function(bf) {
  if (is.infinite(bf) || bf >= 1e4) return("$\\geq$ 10,000")
  paste("=", format(signif(bf, 2), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE))
}
bf_label <- function(bf) {
  if (is.infinite(bf) || bf > 100) "decisive"
  else if (bf > 10) "strong"
  else if (bf > 3) "moderate"
  else "anecdotal"
}
# Drift rows of a fit as prose, for whatever stimulus factor the fit carries
.drift_labels <- c(high = "HF", low = "LF", very_low = "VLF", nonword = "NW", word = "word",
                   A = "stimulus A", B = "stimulus B")
.drift_rows <- function(fe) {
  rows <- grep("^drift_", rownames(fe), value = TRUE)
  lbl  <- sub("^drift_(stim_cat|freq|stimulus)", "", rows)
  lbl  <- ifelse(lbl %in% names(.drift_labels), .drift_labels[lbl], lbl)
  list(rows = rows, lbl = unname(lbl))
}
drift_txt <- function(fe, digits = 2) {
  d <- .drift_rows(fe)
  est <- apply(fe[d$rows, , drop = FALSE], 1, fmt_est, digits = digits)
  paste(sprintf("%s %s", d$lbl, est), collapse = "; ")
}
drift_order <- function(fe) {
  d <- .drift_rows(fe)
  paste(d$lbl[order(-fe[d$rows, "Estimate"])], collapse = " > ")
}

# --- Fitted models, lexical decision data ------------------------------------
fit_acc_ezdm       <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc.rds"))
fit_resp_ezdm      <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp.rds"))
fit_acc_ezdm_freq  <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc_freq.rds"))
fit_resp_ezdm_freq <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp_freq.rds"))
fit_cswald_simple  <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_simple.rds"))
fit_cswald_resp    <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_resp.rds"))
fit_ddm_acc        <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_acc.rds"))
fit_ddm_resp       <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_resp.rds"))

# --- Fitted model, simulated data (supplementary recovery study) -------------
fit_cswald_crisk <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_crisk.rds"))
true_params      <- read_csv(here("data", "true_parameters.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)

# Cached prepared datasets, used to display the required data formats
data_accuracy_clean <- read_csv(here("data", "lexical_accuracy_triallevel.csv"),
                                show_col_types = FALSE)
data_acc_ezdm <- read_csv(here("data", "lexical_accuracy_ezdm3par.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE)
data_response_clean <- read_csv(here("data", "lexical_response_triallevel.csv"),
                                show_col_types = FALSE)

# --- Tutorial 1: EZ-Diffusion 3par (accuracy-coded) --------------------------
fe_t1 <- fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)
t1_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_acc_ezdm), na.rm = TRUE)
t1_ess  <- min(summary(fit_acc_ezdm)$fixed[, "Bulk_ESS"], na.rm = TRUE)
t1_time <- fit_time(fit_acc_ezdm)
# Divergent transitions across the eight lexical fits. The text states that
# none occurred, so the guard fails the render if a refit ever changes that.
.n_div <- function(fit) {
  np <- brms::nuts_params(fit)
  sum(np$Value[np$Parameter == "divergent__"])
}
n_div_all <- sum(sapply(list(fit_acc_ezdm, fit_resp_ezdm, fit_acc_ezdm_freq,
                             fit_resp_ezdm_freq, fit_cswald_simple, fit_cswald_resp,
                             fit_ddm_acc, fit_ddm_resp,
                             readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp_freq_mix.rds"))),
                        .n_div))
stopifnot(n_div_all == 0)
t1_drift_word    <- fmt_est(fe_t1["drift_stim_catword", ])
t1_drift_nonword <- fmt_est(fe_t1["drift_stim_catnonword", ])
t1_bound_speed   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t1_bound_acc     <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t1_ndt           <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
# Equality hypotheses: Evid.Ratio is the Savage-Dickey BF *for* equality;
# its inverse quantifies the evidence against equality (reported as BF in text)
# Savage-Dickey evidence ratios vary slightly between hypothesis() calls, so
# each test is computed once with the seed argument; the printed output and
# the prose both read from that one object.
t1_hyp <- hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, c(
  drift = "drift_stim_catword = drift_stim_catnonword",
  bound = "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed"
), seed = 2026)
t1_bf_drift <- 1 / t1_hyp$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio[1]
t1_bf_bound <- 1 / t1_hyp$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio[2]

# --- Tutorial 1, frequency refit: EZ-Diffusion 3par with freq on drift -------
fe_t4f   <- fixef(fit_acc_ezdm_freq)
t1f_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_acc_ezdm_freq), na.rm = TRUE)
t1f_time <- fit_time(fit_acc_ezdm_freq)
t1f_hyp <- hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm_freq,
                      c(high_vs_very_low = "drift_freqhigh = drift_freqvery_low"),
                      seed = 2026)
t1f_bf_drift <- 1 / t1f_hyp$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t1f_drift_order <- drift_order(fe_t4f)

# --- Tutorial 2: EZ-Diffusion 4par (response-coded) --------------------------
fe_t2 <- fixef(fit_resp_ezdm)
t2_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_resp_ezdm), na.rm = TRUE)
t2_drift_word    <- fmt_est(fe_t2["drift_stim_catword", ])
t2_drift_nonword <- fmt_est(fe_t2["drift_stim_catnonword", ])
t2_zr_speed <- round(plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Estimate"]), 3)
t2_zr_acc   <- round(plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Estimate"]), 3)
t2_zr_speed_ci <- sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Estimate"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Q2.5"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Q97.5"]))
t2_zr_acc_ci <- sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Estimate"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Q2.5"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Q97.5"]))
t2_hyp_drift_word <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "drift_stim_catword = 0", seed = 2026)
t2_bf_drift_word  <- 1 / t2_hyp_drift_word$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t2_hyp_drift_nw   <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "drift_stim_catnonword = 0", seed = 2026)
t2_bf_drift_nw    <- 1 / t2_hyp_drift_nw$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t2_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed",
                           seed = 2026)
t2_bf_bound  <- 1 / t2_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
# The starting point itself: zr = 0 on the logit scale is zeta_r = 0.5, an
# unbiased start. The inverse Evid.Ratio is the BF *against* an unbiased start
# (values below 1 favour it), which is what decides 3par vs 4par.
t2_hyp_zr <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, c(
  accuracy = "zr_conditionaccuracy = 0",
  speed    = "zr_conditionspeed = 0"
), seed = 2026)
t2_bf_zr_acc   <- 1 / t2_hyp_zr$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio[1]
t2_bf_zr_speed <- 1 / t2_hyp_zr$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio[2]
# Minority-boundary counts quoted under Trial-Count Constraint: "word" responses
# to nonwords under accuracy emphasis, per participant, in the data Tutorial 2 fits
.t2_minority <- data_response_clean |>
  dplyr::filter(stim_cat == "nonword", condition == "accuracy") |>
  dplyr::summarise(n_word = sum(response == "upper"), .by = id)
t2_minority_median <- median(.t2_minority$n_word)
t2_minority_min    <- min(.t2_minority$n_word)

# --- Part II: trial-level fits (cswald simple + crisk, ddm acc + resp) -------
fe_t3s <- fixef(fit_cswald_simple)
fe_t3c <- fixef(fit_cswald_resp)
fe_t4a <- fixef(fit_ddm_acc)
fe_t4r <- fixef(fit_ddm_resp)
t3_rhat_simple <- max(brms::rhat(fit_cswald_simple), na.rm = TRUE)
t3_rhat_crisk  <- max(brms::rhat(fit_cswald_resp), na.rm = TRUE)
t4_rhat_acc  <- max(brms::rhat(fit_ddm_acc), na.rm = TRUE)
t4_rhat_resp <- max(brms::rhat(fit_ddm_resp), na.rm = TRUE)
# Minimum bulk ESS over the population-level parameters of the four trial-level fits
.ess_min <- function(f) min(summary(f)$fixed[, "Bulk_ESS"], na.rm = TRUE)
t3_ess_min <- round(min(.ess_min(fit_cswald_simple), .ess_min(fit_cswald_resp),
                        .ess_min(fit_ddm_acc), .ess_min(fit_ddm_resp)))
# x2: cswald "simple" estimates bound on the single-boundary scale (see the
# Censored-Shifted Wald section), so double it to report the full separation.
t3s_bound_acc   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t3s["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) * 2)
t3s_bound_speed <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t3s["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) * 2)
t3s_ndt         <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t3s["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
# The simple version's drift has a log link (all other fits: identity), so its
# drift rows are back-transformed before they are printed or compared
fe_t3s_nat <- fe_t3s
.sd_rows <- grep("^drift_", rownames(fe_t3s_nat))
fe_t3s_nat[.sd_rows, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")] <- exp(fe_t3s[.sd_rows, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")])
t3s_drift_txt   <- drift_txt(fe_t3s_nat)
t3c_zr_speed <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t3c["zr_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t3c_zr_acc   <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t3c["zr_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t3_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_cswald_simple, "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed",
                           seed = 2026)
t3_bf_bound  <- 1 / t3_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t4_bound_acc   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t4_bound_speed <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t4_ndt         <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_drift_txt   <- drift_txt(fe_t4a)
t4_zr_speed <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t4r["zr_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_zr_acc   <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t4r["zr_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_ddm_acc, "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed",
                           seed = 2026)
t4_bf_bound  <- 1 / t4_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t4_hyp_drift <- hypothesis(fit_ddm_acc, "drift_freqhigh = drift_freqvery_low", seed = 2026)
t4_bf_drift  <- 1 / t4_hyp_drift$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
# Lower-boundary (error) counts in the response panel of the trial-level
# checks: observed, and the mean over the same 50 draws script 15 uses (same
# seed and the same order of fits, so the sampled draws are identical).
set.seed(1)
.pp_lower_counts <- function(fit) {
  d  <- sample(ndraws(fit), 50)
  pd <- pp_check(fit, resp_var = "response", draw_ids = d)$data
  k  <- which(pd$x == 0)
  # pd$m carries the quantile name "50%", which c() would append to "pred"
  c(obs = unname(pd$y_obs[k]), pred = round(unname(pd$m[k])))
}
t3s_pp_lower <- .pp_lower_counts(fit_cswald_simple)
t4a_pp_lower <- .pp_lower_counts(fit_ddm_acc)
stopifnot(t3s_pp_lower[["pred"]] < t4a_pp_lower[["pred"]],
          t4a_pp_lower[["pred"]] < t4a_pp_lower[["obs"]])

# --- Part III: EZ-Diffusion (freq) vs full DDM ---------------------------------
t4_ndt_ez  <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4f["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_ndt_ddm <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
.drift_lvls   <- c("freqhigh", "freqlow", "freqvery_low", "freqnonword")
.drift_ratios <- fe_t4f[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"] /
                 fe_t4a[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"]
t4_drift_pct_mean <- round((mean(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)
t4_drift_pct_lo   <- round((min(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)
t4_drift_pct_hi   <- round((max(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)

# Computational cost, read from the archived fits
.ezdm_secs <- purrr::map_dbl(list(fit_acc_ezdm, fit_resp_ezdm, fit_acc_ezdm_freq, fit_resp_ezdm_freq), fit_secs)
.fmt_secs  <- function(s) if (s < 90) sprintf("%.0f s", s) else if (s < 3600) sprintf("%.1f min", s / 60) else sprintf("%.1f h", s / 3600)
cost_ezdm_range     <- paste(.fmt_secs(min(.ezdm_secs)), "to", .fmt_secs(max(.ezdm_secs)))
cost_cswald_simple  <- fit_time(fit_cswald_simple)
cost_cswald_crisk   <- fit_time(fit_cswald_resp)
.ddm_secs <- purrr::map_dbl(list(fit_ddm_acc, fit_ddm_resp), fit_secs)
cost_ddm_range      <- paste(.fmt_secs(min(.ddm_secs)), "to", .fmt_secs(max(.ddm_secs)))
cost_factor         <- paste0("roughly ", format(signif(fit_secs(fit_ddm_acc) / fit_secs(fit_acc_ezdm_freq), 2), big.mark = ","))
cost_simple_share   <- round(100 * fit_secs(fit_cswald_simple) / fit_secs(fit_ddm_acc))
cost_crisk_share    <- round(100 * fit_secs(fit_cswald_resp) / fit_secs(fit_ddm_resp))

# --- Part III: orderings the prose states ---------------------------------------
# Each stopifnot() guards a sentence in the text: if a refit changes the ordering,
# the render fails instead of printing a claim the fits no longer support.
fe_t2f <- fixef(fit_resp_ezdm_freq)
.bnd   <- function(fe, cond, m = 1) exp(fe[paste0("bound_condition", cond), "Estimate"]) * m
.pct   <- function(num, den) round((num / den - 1) * 100)
.conds <- c(accuracy = "accuracy", speed = "speed")
.ref_bound <- c(accuracy = 1.59, speed = 0.84)  # Wagenmakers et al. (2008), s = 1
bound_simple_excess <- sapply(.conds, \(c) .pct(.bnd(fe_t3s, c, 2), .bnd(fe_t4a, c)))
bound_ez_deficit    <- sapply(.conds, \(c) -.pct(.bnd(fe_t4f, c), .bnd(fe_t4a, c)))
bound_ez4_deficit   <- sapply(.conds, \(c) -.pct(.bnd(fe_t2f, c), .bnd(fe_t4r, c)))
# The same 4par fit from mixture moments (script 15 section 1.3): how much of
# the gap to the full DDM is the robust-moment offset rather than the approach
fit_resp_ezdm_freq_mix <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp_freq_mix.rds"))
fe_t2fm   <- fixef(fit_resp_ezdm_freq_mix)
t2fm_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_resp_ezdm_freq_mix), na.rm = TRUE)
stopifnot(t2fm_rhat < 1.01)
bound_ez4mix_deficit <- sapply(.conds, \(c) -.pct(.bnd(fe_t2fm, c), .bnd(fe_t4r, c)))
bound_ez4_offset_pts <- bound_ez4_deficit - bound_ez4mix_deficit
# The text says the mixture fit narrows the gap but does not close it
stopifnot(all(bound_ez4_offset_pts > 0), all(bound_ez4mix_deficit > 0))
mix_fallback <- read_csv(here("data", "lexical_response_ezdm4par_freq_mix_fallback.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
bound_crisk_diff    <- max(abs(sapply(.conds, \(c) .pct(.bnd(fe_t3c, c), .bnd(fe_t4r, c)))))
.ndt <- function(fe) exp(fe["ndt_Intercept", "Estimate"])
.simple_drift_ratio <- fe_t3s_nat[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"] /
                       fe_t4a[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"]
simple_drift_lo <- round((min(.simple_drift_ratio) - 1) * 100)
simple_drift_hi <- round((max(.simple_drift_ratio) - 1) * 100)
.word_order <- function(fe) all(diff(fe[paste0("drift_freq", c("high", "low", "very_low")), "Estimate"]) < 0)
stopifnot(
  # bound: EZ-Diffusion < full DDM < doubled simple cswald, in both conditions
  all(sapply(.conds, \(c) .bnd(fe_t4f, c) < .bnd(fe_t4a, c) && .bnd(fe_t4a, c) < .bnd(fe_t3s, c, 2))),
  bound_simple_excess["speed"] > bound_simple_excess["accuracy"],
  # EZ-Diffusion bound closest to the published values
  all(sapply(.conds, \(c) abs(.bnd(fe_t4f, c) - .ref_bound[c]) < abs(.bnd(fe_t4a, c) - .ref_bound[c]))),
  # ndt: EZ-Diffusion > full DDM > simple cswald
  .ndt(fe_t4f) > .ndt(fe_t4a), .ndt(fe_t4a) > .ndt(fe_t3s),
  # EZ-Diffusion drift at or above the full DDM's, most for high-frequency words
  min(.drift_ratios) > 0.99, which.max(.drift_ratios) == 1,
  # simple cswald drift above the full DDM's, furthest for very-low-frequency words
  all(.simple_drift_ratio > 1), which.max(.simple_drift_ratio) == 3,
  # word-frequency order of drift (high > low > very low) in all three approaches
  .word_order(fe_t4f), .word_order(fe_t3s), .word_order(fe_t4a),
  # bound higher under accuracy than speed emphasis in all five lexical fits
  all(sapply(list(fe_t4f, fe_t3s, fe_t4a, fe_t3c, fe_t4r, fe_t2f),
             \(fe) .bnd(fe, "accuracy") > .bnd(fe, "speed")))
)

# Cells that entered the 4par fits (robust moments are NA below min_trials)
lex_cells        <- nrow(dplyr::distinct(data_accuracy_clean, id, condition, stim_cat))
lex_cells_freq   <- nrow(dplyr::distinct(data_accuracy_clean, id, condition, freq))
t2_cells         <- nrow(fit_resp_ezdm$data)

# Cells with a boundary whose RT summaries are unusable: bmm keeps these
# and they enter through their response counts only. The indicator columns bmm
# adds to the data are 0 for such a boundary, so the count is read off the fit.
.counts_only <- function(fit)
  sum(fit$data$rt_used_upper == 0 | fit$data$rt_used_lower == 0)
t2_cells_counts_only <- .counts_only(fit_resp_ezdm)

# Posterior predictive checks of the two EZ-Diffusion fits: design cells whose
# observed statistic falls outside its 90% predictive interval, per observable.
# Same seed, draws, and order as scripts 11 and 12, so the counts match the figures.
.ppc_outside <- function(fit) {
  v <- pp_check_vars(fit)$resp_var
  set.seed(1)
  d <- sample(ndraws(fit), 50)
  sapply(v, \(r) {
    # type = "intervals" is required here: the default view for the ezdm RT
    # statistics is a density overlay, whose $data has no y_obs/ll/hh columns,
    # so the comparison below would silently count 0 cells for every statistic.
    pd <- suppressWarnings(
      pp_check(fit, resp_var = r, draw_ids = d, type = "intervals")
    )$data
    sum(pd$y_obs < pd$ll | pd$y_obs > pd$hh)
  })
}
t1_ppc_out  <- .ppc_outside(fit_acc_ezdm)
t1f_ppc_out <- .ppc_outside(fit_acc_ezdm_freq)
t2_ppc_out  <- .ppc_outside(fit_resp_ezdm)
# The same per-cell check for the four trial-level fits (script 15, section
# 2b, from the same 50 draws as their composite figure), read for the Part III
# table that puts all three approaches through one criterion
trial_ppc <- read_csv(here("data", "trial_level_ppc_cell_counts.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot("var_rt_below" %in% names(trial_ppc))  # direction of the variance misses (script 15)
.tp_count <- function(lbl, col) trial_ppc[[col]][trial_ppc$fit == lbl]
.tp_fits <- c(simple = "Censored-Shifted Wald (simple), accuracy-coded",
              ddm_acc = "Full DDM, accuracy-coded",
              crisk = "Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk), response-coded",
              ddm_resp = "Full DDM, response-coded")
stopifnot(all(.tp_fits %in% trial_ppc$fit),
          all(trial_ppc$cells == lex_cells_freq))
# The text says the trial-level fits miss at least as many cells as the EZ
# refit and that RT variance is where each of them misses most
stopifnot(.tp_count(.tp_fits[["ddm_acc"]], "mean_rt") >= t1f_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]],
          .tp_count(.tp_fits[["ddm_acc"]], "var_rt")  >= t1f_ppc_out[["var_rt"]],
          .tp_count(.tp_fits[["ddm_acc"]], "p_upper") >= t1f_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]],
          all(trial_ppc$var_rt >= trial_ppc$mean_rt),
          all(trial_ppc$var_rt[trial_ppc$fit != .tp_fits[["simple"]]] >=
              trial_ppc$p_upper[trial_ppc$fit != .tp_fits[["simple"]]]))
ppc_cells_tab <- tibble::tibble(
  Fit = c("EZ-Diffusion Model (3par, frequency refit)", "Censored-Shifted Wald (simple)",
          "Full DDM, accuracy-coded", "Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk)", "Full DDM, response-coded"),
  `Mean RT`     = c(t1f_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]], purrr::map_dbl(.tp_fits, .tp_count, col = "mean_rt")),
  `RT variance` = c(t1f_ppc_out[["var_rt"]], purrr::map_dbl(.tp_fits, .tp_count, col = "var_rt")),
  `Proportion upper` = c(t1f_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]], purrr::map_dbl(.tp_fits, .tp_count, col = "p_upper"))
)

# Lexical-data facts quoted in Part II and III: accuracy-coded error rates by

.err <- data_accuracy_clean |>
  dplyr::summarise(err = 100 * mean(response == "lower"), .by = c(condition, freq)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(err)
.ne <- nrow(.err)

err_second <- sprintf("%.1f", .err$err[.ne - 1])
err_max    <- sprintf("%.1f", .err$err[.ne])

          .err$condition[.ne - 1] == "speed", .err$freq[.ne - 1] == "low",
          .err$condition[.ne] == "speed", .err$freq[.ne] == "very_low",
          .err$err[.ne - 1] < 20, .err$err[.ne] > 20)
min_rt_ms <- round(1000 * min(data_accuracy_clean$rt))
ez4f_cells       <- nrow(fit_resp_ezdm_freq$data)
ez4f_cells_counts_only <- .counts_only(fit_resp_ezdm_freq)
stopifnot(t2_cells_counts_only > 0, t2_cells_counts_only < t2_cells,
          ez4f_cells_counts_only > 0, ez4f_cells_counts_only < ez4f_cells)

# --- Part I: recovery with a biased starting point (scripts/22) ----------------
fit_ezdm_4par_bias <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_4par_bias.rds"))
fit_ezdm_3par_bias <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_3par_bias.rds"))

true_bias <- read_csv(here("data", "true_parameters_bias.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

.nd <- function(fe) fmt_est(exp(fe["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)

# Sentence guards for the Results paragraph (generating values: bound 1.5, ndt 0.3 s, drift +/- 0.6)

bias_time_4par <- fit_time(fit_ezdm_4par_bias); bias_time_3par <- fit_time(fit_ezdm_3par_bias)
bias_time_ddm  <- fit_time(fit_ddm_bias)
# Convergence over all population- and participant-level parameters of the three fits;

.bias_diag <- lapply(list(fit_ezdm_4par_bias, fit_ezdm_3par_bias, fit_ddm_bias), \(f) {

})

}
```

# Introduction

Consider two participants in a speeded choice task, deciding whether a digit is odd or even. Participant A responds correctly in 550 ms on average with 90% accuracy; participant B in 600 ms with 95% accuracy. Who performed better? An analysis of response times favors A, an analysis of accuracy favors B, and neither says *why* the two differ. A may extract evidence faster but set a more liberal decision threshold; B may extract evidence at the same rate but trade speed for accuracy. Mean RT and accuracy confound these processes and are not process-pure measures of either [@frischkorn2026validity].

Evidence accumulation models (EAMs) address this by describing how latent cognitive processes give rise to response times (RTs) and choices. They decompose performance into the rate of evidence accumulation, the amount of evidence required before responding, and the time taken by non-decisional processes such as stimulus encoding and motor execution. Since @ratcliff1978theory, EAMs have become the standard framework for RT data in perception, memory retrieval, and cognitive control [@ratcliff2008diffusion; @donkin2018response; @evans2019evidence]. The Diffusion Decision Model [DDM; @ratcliff1978theory] is the most widely applied EAM for two-choice tasks and is supported by decades of empirical validation [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. Race models and competitive accumulators [@brown2008lba; @rouder2015lnr; @tillman2020racing; @usher2001lca] are beyond the scope of this tutorial [for reviews, see @ratcliff2004comparison; @forstmann2016review; @boag2025expert].

Within the DDM framework, several estimation approaches extract the same core parameters, drift, boundary separation, non-decision time, and optionally the relative starting point, from data at different levels of granularity: from summary statistics per condition, or from trial-level RT distributions through a distributional approximation or the exact Wiener first-passage time likelihood [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @anders2016shifted; @vandekerckhove2007fitting]. The approaches differ in data requirements, computational cost, and assumptions, and contaminant responses such as premature responses or attentional lapses bias them to different degrees [@ratcliff2002estimating; @ratcliff2008ez; @boag2025expert].

Until recently, each approach required its own software, which made comparing them on the same data laborious. The `bmm` R package [@frischkorn2025tutorial] implements all three in one Bayesian hierarchical framework built on `brms` [@burkner2017brms] and Stan [@cmdstanr2024]: the EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm`) [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion], the Censored-Shifted Wald (`cswald`) [@anders2016shifted] as a distributional proxy, and full DDM likelihood estimation (`ddm`). Switching between them changes only the model object; the formula syntax, prior specification, and post-processing tools stay the same.[^future]

[^future]: The implementation of race-model architectures in `bmm` may follow in future versions of the package.

Hierarchical estimation borrows information across participants, which stabilizes individual estimates at moderate trial counts [@vandekerckhove2011hierarchical], propagates uncertainty instead of testing point estimates in a second step, and handles the unbalanced cells that arise when some conditions produce few errors [@boehm2018shortcuts]. For the EZ-Diffusion Model the consequences are largest. Originally a calculator that turns three summary statistics into three parameters, it becomes, once recast as a likelihood [@chavez2025ez], a hierarchical model that accepts predictors on any parameter, and it keeps its speed: the fits in this tutorial take seconds to minutes where the full DDM takes hours. This is the central message of the tutorial. On the lexical decision data analyzed here, the condition effects the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model found agreed in sign, rank order, and evidence category with the full DDM's, at a fraction of the cost; the absolute values of boundary separation and non-decision time did not. That is one dataset and two large effects, so the comparison illustrates the case rather than settling it, and Part III states what it does and does not show.

This tutorial is written for researchers with basic familiarity with R and with hierarchical regression models in `brms` who have collected or plan to collect two-choice RT data. After completing it, you will be able to:

1. Preprocess RT data to detect and handle contaminant responses with `bmm`'s dedicated functions.
2. Specify, fit, and evaluate the EZ-Diffusion Model as a primary analysis of condition effects on drift, boundary separation, and non-decision time; extend it to response bias with the four-parameter version; and judge when the starting point has to be estimated rather than fixed.
3. Fit the trial-level approaches, the Censored-Shifted Wald and the full DDM, at the same specification.
4. Decide which approach your research question needs, and read the differences between them.

Part I introduces the EZ-Diffusion Model on the classic lexical decision data of @wagenmakers2008lexical and adds a parameter recovery study with a biased starting point. Part II fits the Censored-Shifted Wald and the full DDM at the specification Part I arrived at. Part III compares the three approaches and turns the comparison into practical guidelines. Throughout, the tutorial covers the simple four-parameter DDM for two-choice tasks. Between-trial variability parameters, race architectures, multi-alternative tasks, and formal model comparison (leave-one-out cross-validation, bridge sampling) are available via `brms` or other packages but are beyond its scope.

# Background: Evidence Accumulation Models

## The Diffusion Model Framework

In a lexical decision task, a participant sees the letter string "CHAIR" and presses one of two buttons to classify it as a word or a nonword. From stimulus onset, evidence such as orthographic regularity, phonological plausibility, or lexical familiarity accumulates noisily toward one of two response boundaries. Reaching the "word" boundary first produces a "word" response, reaching the "nonword" boundary a "nonword" response. The observed RT is this decision time plus non-decisional components such as stimulus encoding and motor execution (@fig-diffusion-schematic).

```{r}
#| label: fig-diffusion-schematic
#| fig-cap: "Schematic of the Diffusion Decision Model"
#| apa-note: "Evidence accumulates noisily from the starting point ($\\zeta_r$) toward one of two response boundaries separated by distance $\\alpha$, with the mean rate of accumulation given by the drift ($\\delta$). Accumulation begins only once the stimulus has been encoded (shaded region) and the response is registered only after motor execution (dashed segments): the non-decision time $\\tau$ is the sum of these two intervals. Because the model estimates only that sum, the split drawn here is illustrative. Several example paths are shown (blue: reaching the upper boundary, correct response; red: reaching the lower boundary, error). The distributions attached to each boundary show the resulting response times, right-skewed for correct responses and errors alike (the error distribution's height is exaggerated for visibility)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "03_diffusion_schematic.pdf"))
```

The four parameters of the DDM [@ratcliff1978theory; @ratcliff2008diffusion] each capture one aspect of this process:

- Drift ($\delta$ or `drift`): The mean rate of evidence accumulation, reflecting stimulus quality or strength. Higher drift yields faster and more accurate responses.
- Boundary separation ($\alpha$ or `bound`): The distance between the two response boundaries, capturing *response caution*. Wider boundaries require more evidence, yielding slower but more accurate responses.
- Non-decision time ($\tau$ or `ndt`): The portion of the observed RT not attributable to the decision process, encompassing *stimulus encoding*, which precedes evidence accumulation, and *motor execution*, which follows it. Only the sum of the two is estimated; the model does not separate them.
- Relative starting point ($\zeta_r$ or `zr`): The starting point of evidence accumulation between the two boundaries, expressed as a proportion of the boundary separation (0.5 = unbiased). Values deviating from 0.5 indicate an *a priori response bias* toward the upper or lower response.

A fifth quantity, the diffusion noise $s$, sets the scale of the other parameters and is fixed at 1 throughout this tutorial, the standard choice in the literature. Estimating it alongside the others under-identifies the model unless drift or boundary separation is fixed instead [@nunez2025identifiable].

Because each parameter corresponds to a distinct process, experimental manipulations should affect them selectively: stimulus quality (degradation, word frequency) should change drift but not boundary separation or non-decision time, and speed–accuracy instructions should change boundary separation alone [@voss2004interpreting; @ratcliff2008diffusion]. Evidence for such *selective influence* is central to the validity of the DDM [see @boag2025expert, Table 2, for an overview].

This four-parameter formulation is the *simple* DDM. The *full* DDM [@ratcliff2002estimating] adds trial-to-trial variability in drift, starting point, and non-decision time, which accounts for slow errors, fast errors, and variation in the leading edge of the RT distribution. The added parameters are hard to recover [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @boehm2018variability], and hierarchical fits of the full DDM are rarely feasible beyond small designs.[^feasibility] For detecting condition effects on drift or bound, the simple DDM is the more parsimonious and statistically powerful choice [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. All three estimation approaches in `bmm` are therefore based on it.

[^feasibility]: In the collaborative estimation exercise of @boehm2018variability, a hierarchical dataset of 20 simulated participants with one difficulty manipulation was at the edge of what expert teams could fit: one hierarchical fit took about 14 hours on four cores, another team ran a single chain, and a third abandoned hierarchical estimation. Amortized inference with neural networks moves this cost into a one-time training phase and has been applied to millions of participants [@vonkrause2026scaling], but it returns to two-step inference, with parameters estimated per participant and related to predictors afterwards.

## DDM Estimation Approaches in bmm

The `bmm` package implements three approaches for estimating DDM parameters that share the same theoretical framework but differ in data requirements and computational cost. @tbl-model-comparison summarizes the differences; the distributions named in its Likelihood row are unpacked in the subsections that follow.

| Feature | EZ-Diffusion Model | Censored-Shifted Wald | Full DDM |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `bmm` function | `ezdm()` | `cswald()` | `ddm()` |
| Data required | Aggregated per cell: mean RT, RT variance, accuracy | Trial-level: RT, response | Trial-level: RT, response |
| Likelihood | Closed-form EZ equations | Shifted Wald, errors censored (simple) or racing accumulators (crisk) | Wiener first-passage time |
| Min trials/cell | ~30 (3par); ~30 per boundary (4par) | ~50 | ~50 |
| Fitting time | `r cost_ezdm_range` | `r cost_cswald_simple` (simple), `r cost_cswald_crisk` (crisk) | `r cost_ddm_range` |
| Best suited for | Primary analysis of condition effects and individual differences; exploration across many conditions | Trial-level analysis of high-accuracy data (< ~20% errors), including iterative model development (simple); response bias when errors are frequent (crisk) | Questions that need trial-level information: RT-distribution shape, trial-level predictors, absolute values of bound and ndt |

: Summary of the three DDM Estimation Approaches in `bmm` {#tbl-model-comparison apa-note="Parameter symbols used throughout: drift $\delta$, boundary separation (bound) $\alpha$, non-decision time (ndt) $\tau$, relative starting point $\zeta_r$. Fitting times are wall-clock times of the slowest chain on the lexical decision data (Part III), measured on an Apple M3 Max with five chains, two threads per chain, and one fit at a time."}

### EZ-Diffusion Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm` in `bmm`) [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion] made diffusion model analysis quick by eliminating iterative fitting. For a diffusion process with an unbiased starting point and $s = 1$, the probability of reaching the upper boundary, the mean decision time (MDT), and the variance of the decision time (VDT) have closed-form expressions in drift $\delta$ and bound $\alpha$ alone. With $y = -\alpha\delta$:

$$
P(\text{upper}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{y}}, \qquad
\text{MDT} = \frac{\alpha}{2\delta} \cdot \frac{1 - e^{y}}{1 + e^{y}}, \qquad
\text{VDT} = \frac{\alpha}{2\delta^{3}} \cdot \frac{2y e^{y} - e^{2y} + 1}{(1 + e^{y})^{2}}
$$

The observed mean RT is MDT plus ndt; the observed RT variance is VDT, because a constant ndt shifts the distribution without spreading it. The original formulation inverted these expressions, turning three summary statistics per cell into three parameters by calculation rather than by fitting.

`bmm` runs the equations forward instead, following the probabilistic reformulation of @chavez2025ez: the three summary statistics of each cell are treated as noisy observations of the values the model predicts for them. The response count is binomial, and the mean and variance of the RTs follow the joint sampling distribution of the mean and variance of $n$ decision times, which depends on the first four cumulants the DDM implies for the current parameters. @srivastava2016moments [Eq. 28] give the cumulant generating function of the decision time conditional on the response; `bmm` derives the third and fourth cumulant from it. The Appendix states the resulting likelihood. Specifying the model this way makes hierarchical estimation with regression structures on every parameter possible, and it makes the dependence on preprocessing explicit: the data entering the likelihood are $n_{\text{upper}}$, $\overline{\text{RT}}$, and $s^{2}_{\text{RT}}$, so whatever distorts those statistics distorts the estimates.

The speed has two costs: no trial-to-trial variability can be estimated, and the starting point is assumed unbiased unless the four-parameter version is used. The model nevertheless detects condition effects with statistical power comparable to or higher than the full DDM's in prior simulations [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @wagenmakers2008extensions]. `bmm` includes two extensions. *Robust-EZ* [@wagenmakers2008extensions] fits a two-component mixture, a uniform distribution for contaminant RTs and an ex-Gaussian for the decision process, and feeds the ex-Gaussian component's mean and variance into the equations instead of the raw sample moments; it is the mixture method of `ezdm_summary_stats()` introduced in the Data Preprocessing section. The four-parameter version estimates the relative starting point from the mean and variance of RTs computed separately for upper- and lower-boundary responses [@grasman2009ez; @srivastava2016moments]; Tutorial 2 shows it.

### Censored-Shifted Wald Model

The Censored-Shifted Wald (`cswald` in `bmm`) [@anders2016shifted] models individual RTs, so it preserves distributional information and takes trial-level predictors, while remaining faster than the full DDM. It uses the shifted Wald (inverse Gaussian) distribution, the first-passage time of a diffusion process with a single *absorbing* boundary, one at which the process stops as soon as it arrives [@anders2016shifted]. When errors are rare, because drift is high, bound is wide, or responses are biased toward the correct boundary, the decision process behaves as if only one boundary existed, and the shifted Wald parameters closely approximate those of the DDM [@miller2018shifted].

`bmm` implements the two versions of @miller2018shifted, which differ in how they treat errors. The *simple* version treats an error as a *censored* correct response: the trial says only that the correct-boundary process had not finished by the observed RT. A correct response at time $t$ therefore contributes the shifted Wald density $f$, and an error contributes the survival function $S(t) = 1 - F(t)$, the probability that the correct-boundary process had not finished by $t$:

$$
\mathcal{L}(t) =
\begin{cases}
f(t \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau) & \text{correct response} \\[4pt]
S(t \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau) = 1 - \displaystyle\int_{\tau}^{t} f(u \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau)\, du & \text{error}
\end{cases}
$$

with the shifted Wald density

$$
f(t \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau) = \frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{2\pi (t - \tau)^{3}}} \, \exp\!\left(-\frac{\big(\alpha - \delta (t-\tau)\big)^{2}}{2 (t - \tau)}\right), \qquad t > \tau
$$

and $s = 1$. Here $\alpha$ is the distance from the starting point to the single boundary, not the separation between two boundaries. With an unbiased starting point the two differ by a factor of 2, and `bmm` reports the simple version's bound on the single-boundary scale: double it before comparing it with `ezdm`, `ddm`, or the competing-risks version. Errors are used, not discarded, but a censored trial bounds the completion time only from below and constrains the parameters less than a completed trial does, so the approximation degrades as errors become frequent. @miller2018shifted recommend the simple version for error rates below 20%.

The *competing-risks* (crisk) version models correct and error RTs explicitly, as two racing shifted Wald accumulators that share one non-decision time; the first to finish produces the response. Nothing is left as a lower bound, which removes the error-rate guideline and makes the relative starting point estimable, and at higher error rates this version approximates the Wiener distribution better [@miller2018shifted].

### The Full DDM

`ddm()` uses the Wiener first-passage time distribution to model the RT and the boundary reached jointly [@ratcliff1978theory; @vandekerckhove2007fitting]. Unlike the Censored-Shifted Wald, it implements the two-boundary process directly, capturing the probability of reaching each boundary and the complete distribution of times to reach it. The price is that the density has no closed form: the first-passage density at the upper boundary is an infinite series in $\alpha$, $\delta$, $\zeta_r$, and $t - \tau$ [@navarro2009fast], and the lower-boundary density follows by replacing $\delta$ with $-\delta$ and $\zeta_r$ with $1 - \zeta_r$, which is what `bmm` does.[^absolute-z] Every likelihood evaluation truncates the series, switching adaptively between a large-time and a small-time expansion [@navarro2009fast], so each evaluation costs far more than for `ezdm` or `cswald`. Earlier estimation methods include $\chi^2$ fitting [@ratcliff2002estimating], maximum likelihood [@vandekerckhove2007fitting; @voss2007fastdm], and hierarchical Bayesian samplers [@vandekerckhove2011hierarchical; @wiecki2013hddm]; `bmm` fits the full DDM with Stan's `wiener_lpdf()` inside the same hierarchical framework as the other two approaches.

[^absolute-z]: Much of the literature states this substitution on the absolute scale: with $z = \alpha\zeta_r$, the lower-boundary density follows by replacing $\delta$ with $-\delta$ and $z$ with $\alpha - z$. The two are the same substitution, since $(\alpha - z)/\alpha = 1 - \zeta_r$. We use the relative form because $\zeta_r$ is what `bmm` estimates and reports.

## Estimating DDM Parameters with Existing Software

Most established packages implement one approach: `fast-dm` fits the full DDM by $\chi^2$ or maximum likelihood [@voss2007fastdm], HDDM estimates it hierarchically in Python [@wiecki2013hddm], `rtdists` provides DDM and LBA densities in R [@singmann2016rtdists], and the EZ-Diffusion equations circulate as spreadsheets and scripts [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion]. The exception, and the closest point of comparison, is the R package `EMC2` [@stevenson2026emc2], a general hierarchical Bayesian framework for evidence accumulation models. @tbl-software summarizes how the packages relate to `bmm`.[^development]

[^development]: Both `EMC2` and `bmm` are comparatively new packages under active development. The features compared in @tbl-software are those available at the time of writing; both can be expected to grow.

| Feature | `fast-dm`, `rtdists` | Standalone EZ-Diffusion | HDDM | `EMC2` | `bmm` |
|:--------------|:---------------|:---------------|:--------------|:--------------------|:--------------------|
| Estimation | Maximum likelihood or $\chi^2$ | Closed-form calculation | Hierarchical Bayesian | Hierarchical Bayesian | Hierarchical Bayesian |
| Sampler | Numerical optimization | None | Slice sampling (PyMC) | Particle Metropolis-within-Gibbs | Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan) |
| Uncertainty | Point estimates (+ bootstrap) | Point estimates | Posterior distributions | Posterior distributions | Posterior distributions |
| Multiple conditions | Fit separately per condition | Computed separately per cell | Regression syntax | Formula per parameter (`design()`) | Formula per parameter (`bmf()`) |
| Inference over conditions | Stepwise | Stepwise | One step | One step | One step |
| Continuous predictors | No | No | Limited | Yes | Yes |
| Predictors per parameter | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Grouping factors | None | None | Participants | Participants | Any `brms` structure (participants, items, crossed) |
| Parameter covariance | No | No | No | Full, blocked, diagonal, or factor-analytic | Optional, via linked terms |
| Trials per cell | Several hundred | ~30 | ~50 | ~50 | ~30 (`ezdm`) to ~50 (trial-level) |
| Models covered | Full DDM | EZ-Diffusion | Full DDM | Full DDM, LBA, RDM, LNR, custom likelihoods | Three DDM approaches, one interface |
| Post-processing | Package-specific | Manual | Package-specific | Package-specific | The `brms` ecosystem |

: Comparison of `bmm` With Existing Software for Estimating DDM Parameters {#tbl-software apa-note="`fast-dm` and `rtdists` fit each participant separately by maximum likelihood (ML). Stepwise: effects tested on point estimates, ignoring their uncertainty [@boehm2018shortcuts]. Sampler of `EMC2`: @gunawan2020pmwg. Four-parameter `ezdm`: ~30 trials per boundary."}

`EMC2` covers far more of the EAM family: the full DDM with its variability parameters, the linear ballistic accumulator, racing diffusion and lognormal race models, and user-supplied likelihoods, and it estimates a covariance matrix across participants' parameters. `bmm` implements only the simple DDM, partly because Stan requires a differentiable likelihood. What `bmm` offers is the `brms` idiom: one formula per parameter in `brms` syntax, with its random-effects, prior, and post-processing ecosystem; any grouping factor as a random effect, so the lexical decision data below could carry by-word random effects alongside by-participant ones; and the EZ-Diffusion and Censored-Shifted Wald approaches next to the full DDM behind one interface, which is what makes the staged workflow of this tutorial possible. If your question concerns a race architecture, the variability parameters, or how parameters covary across people, `EMC2` is the better tool. If your work sits in the mixed-model idiom or spans several measurement models [@frischkorn2025tutorial; @frischkorn2026m3], `bmm` is.

## The `bmm` Workflow

Fitting any of the three models in `bmm` follows the same three steps:

1. Define the model: A model constructor (`ezdm()`, `cswald()`, or `ddm()`) returns a model object that names the data columns holding the required response variables and selects the model version.
2. Specify predictor formulas: `bmmformula()`, or its shorthand `bmf()`, gives each model parameter its own `brms` formula [@burkner2017brms], including random effects.
3. Fit the model: `bmm()` takes the model object, the formula, and the data, translates them into a `brms` model, and hands it to Stan.

You provide two things: the names of the required variables in your data, and how parameters vary over conditions. `bmm` supplies the likelihood, fixes the parameters a version does not estimate, sets the link functions, chooses weakly informative default priors, and checks the data before fitting. The relationship between `bmm` and `brms` is that between `brms` and Stan: each layer removes boilerplate from the one below without hiding it, and both the `brms` object and the Stan code remain inspectable.

One convention first: RTs must be in seconds, as in nearly all DDM software, because the parameters and their default priors are on that scale. `bmm` does not inspect or convert the RT scale, so divide millisecond data by 1000 before fitting.

Because `bmm` builds on `brms`, fitted models use the `brms` post-processing ecosystem: `summary()` for estimates and convergence diagnostics, `pp_check()` for posterior predictive checks of every observable of the likelihood (selected with `resp_var`), `fixef()` and `ranef()` for parameter summaries, and `hypothesis()` for Bayes factors from Savage-Dickey density ratios. Every tutorial below runs these three steps with a different model object.

# Software and Data

All analyses run in R with `bmm` on the `cmdstanr` backend, which needs a working CmdStan installation (`cmdstanr::install_cmdstan()`). The packages loaded throughout are:

```{r}
#| label: setup-packages
pacman::p_load(here, bmm, brms, cmdstanr, tidyverse, tidybayes, patchwork, rtdists)
```

All analyses use version 1.4.1 of `bmm`, available from CRAN via `install.packages("bmm")`.

# The Lexical Decision Dataset

We use the classic lexical decision study of @wagenmakers2008lexical, available as `speed_acc` in the `rtdists` package [@singmann2016rtdists].[^dataset] It is publicly available, a benchmark in the diffusion modeling literature, has clear EAM predictions, and comes with published parameter estimates as reference values. Seventeen participants classified letter strings as words or nonwords under *speed emphasis* (respond as quickly as possible) and *accuracy emphasis* (respond as accurately as possible). Words were of high, low, or very low frequency, with matched nonwords, giving a 2 (emphasis) × 2 (stimulus category) within-subjects design with approximately 460 trials per cell per participant; the frequency levels split the word cells further from Tutorial 1 onwards. Emphasis should affect bound, and stimulus category, word frequency in particular, should affect drift.

[^dataset]: The columns the tutorial uses are `id` (participant), `rt` (response time in seconds), `condition` (`speed` or `accuracy` emphasis), `stim_cat` (`word` or `nonword`), `frequency` (word frequency), `response` (the key pressed, with `"error"` marking recording failures), and `censor` (trials the original study excluded).

## Data Preparation

We convert factors to character (`response` and `stim_cat` have different level sets), collapse the nonwords into one level of a four-level `freq` factor, and remove 6 recording failures and all trials flagged as `censor`, which the original study excluded. The raw `response` column codes recording failures as `"error"`, not incorrect responses; those are identified below by comparing `response` with `stim_cat`.^[The `censor` flag is unrelated to the statistical *censoring* of error RTs in the Censored-Shifted Wald (Part II). `scripts/01_prepare_lexical_data.R` contains the full data preparation code.]

```{r}
#| label: data-load
data("speed_acc", package = "rtdists")

data_lexical <- speed_acc |>
  mutate(
    response  = as.character(response),
    stim_cat  = as.character(stim_cat),
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("speed", "accuracy")),
    freq = factor(
      ifelse(stim_cat == "nonword", "nonword", as.character(frequency)),
      levels = c("high", "low", "very_low", "nonword")
    )
  ) |>
  filter(response != "error", censor == FALSE)
```

The response variable must be binary, naming the boundary each trial reached. Two codings answer different questions:

- Accuracy coding (upper = correct, lower = error): Drift reflects how quickly evidence for the *correct answer* accumulates. This is the standard approach for testing selective influence.
- Response coding (upper = "word" response, lower = "nonword" response): Drift reflects evidence toward saying *"word"*, positive for word stimuli and negative or near zero for nonwords. The relative starting point ($\zeta_r$) captures response bias toward saying "word".

```{r}
#| label: data-recode
# Accuracy-coded: correct = upper, error = lower
data_accuracy <- data_lexical |>
  mutate(response = ifelse(response == stim_cat, "upper", "lower"))

# Response-coded: "word" response = upper, "nonword" response = lower
data_response <- data_lexical |>
  mutate(response = ifelse(response == "word", "upper", "lower"))
```

# Data Preprocessing: Handling Contaminant Responses

Not all RTs arise from the evidence accumulation process. Premature responses, attentional lapses, and responses given without stimulus information violate the assumption that every RT is a decision time plus a non-decision time [@ratcliff1993methods; @ratcliff2002estimating], and even a few percent of them inflate the boundary separation the EZ-Diffusion Model recovers and distort its drift, more so the higher the contamination rate [@ratcliff2008ez; @wagenmakers2008extensions]. Hard RT cutoffs, such as discarding everything under 200 ms or above 3,000 ms, are arbitrary and biased in their own right, because they truncate legitimate fast and slow responses [@ulrich1994effects]; across a wide range of exclusion rules, the distortion the cure introduces often exceeds the one it removes [@berger2021outlier; @miller2023outlier]. `bmm` provides the model-based alternative of @ratcliff2002estimating and @wagenmakers2008extensions: a mixture in which contaminant RTs follow a uniform distribution and the decision process a right-skewed core distribution, fitted per participant and condition.

## Identifying Contaminant Responses on the Trial Level

`flag_contaminant_rts()` fits the mixture within each cell by expectation–maximization (EM) and returns, for every trial, the probability that it is a contaminant. The core distribution can be ex-Gaussian, lognormal, or inverse Gaussian; we use the ex-Gaussian, the sum of a normally and an exponentially distributed variable, which was the choice of @wagenmakers2008extensions. Applied to the accuracy-coded data per participant, emphasis condition, and stimulus category:

```{r}
#| label: data-flag
data_accuracy <- data_accuracy |>
  group_by(id, condition, stim_cat) |>
  mutate(
    contam_prob = flag_contaminant_rts(
      rt,
      distribution = "exgaussian",
      contaminant_bound = c("min", "max")
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

`contaminant_bound` sets the support of the uniform component, here from the fastest to the slowest RT in the cell, so it absorbs premature and delayed responses alike. When the EM does not converge in a cell, the function warns and returns `NA` for every trial in it, and a filter on the probability then discards the whole cell; the first line of the next chunk stops with an error instead. Trials with `contam_prob > 0.5` are more likely contaminants than legitimate responses under the mixture, and the trial-level approaches of Part II exclude them:

```{r}
#| label: data-clean
stopifnot(!anyNA(data_accuracy$contam_prob))  # no cell may be dropped silently
data_accuracy_clean <- data_accuracy |> filter(contam_prob <= 0.5)
data_response_clean <- data_response |>
  semi_join(data_accuracy_clean, by = c("id", "condition", "stim_cat", "rt"))
```

The `semi_join()` keeps the response-coded trials whose accuracy-coded counterpart survived, so both data frames contain the same trials. The key is not unique, because many trials in a cell share an RT, but under the threshold rule tied trials are kept or dropped together, since the probability depends only on the RT and the cell's fitted mixture. The alternative, excluding each trial with probability equal to its contaminant probability, retains borderline trials in proportion to their uncertainty; `scripts/01_prepare_lexical_data.R` shows it as a commented alternative, which needs a unique trial identifier for the join. Where flagged trials are fast, `validate_fast_guesses()` tests whether they respond at chance, as premature responses should, and returns a Bayes factor for accuracy = 0.5 among them.

## Computing Summary Statistics for the EZ-Diffusion Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model takes, for every cell, the mean RT, the RT variance, the number of upper-boundary responses, and the number of trials. `ezdm_summary_stats()` computes them, and its `method` argument selects how: `simple` returns the sample mean and variance; `robust` the median and $(\mathrm{IQR}/1.349)^2$, where 1.349 is the IQR of a standard normal distribution; and `mixture` fits the same uniform-plus-core mixture as `flag_contaminant_rts()` and returns the mean and variance of the fitted core. The mixture method is the robust-EZ estimator of @wagenmakers2008extensions, and the robust method is the estimator @chavez2026robust proposed for the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model.[^robust-names] We compute the statistics from `data_accuracy_clean`, so that every fit in this tutorial starts from the same trials:

[^robust-names]: The two names are easy to confuse. What @chavez2026robust call the "robust EZ-DDM" is the median/IQR method, `method = "robust"`; what @wagenmakers2008extensions call "robust-EZ" is the mixture method, `method = "mixture"`. They are different estimators.

```{r}
#| label: data-sumstats
data_acc_ezdm <- data_accuracy_clean |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(
      rt, response,
      version      = "3par",
      method       = "mixture",
      distribution = "exgaussian"
    ),
    .by = c(id, condition, stim_cat)
  )
```

`summarize()` spreads the one-row result into columns, and `.by` groups for this one call. The result has one row per *cell*, a participant × emphasis × stimulus-category combination, `r lex_cells` in all (17 × 2 × 2), with the columns `mean_rt`, `var_rt`, `n_upper`, and `n_trials` that `ezdm()` expects and a `contaminant_prop` column with the estimated proportion of contaminants. These four statistics are the entire input to the model; everything else in the raw trials is discarded, which is why the approach is fast and why it cannot take trial-level predictors. Under the mixture method the counts match the moments: `n_upper` and `n_trials` count the responses the core distribution's moments rest on, with the expected contaminants removed and split across the boundaries according to `guess_rate` (0.5 by default), because a response given without stimulus information is correct only by chance. If the EM does not converge in a cell, the function warns, returns the robust statistics for that cell, and sets `contaminant_prop` to `NA`; check that column before fitting. `version = "3par"` pools both boundaries into one mean and one variance per cell; `"4par"` returns them per boundary (Tutorial 2).

## Which Method to Use

I recommend the mixture method with the ex-Gaussian core as the default. It is the robust-EZ procedure of @wagenmakers2008extensions, largely unaffected by contaminants in their simulations where the standard moments were not. The robust statistics are the alternative when the EM cannot converge, which happens in cells with very few trials on one boundary (Tutorial 2), or by preference: @chavez2026robust show that tests of drift effects from the median and IQR are as accurate as tests from the standard moments on clean data and stay accurate under contamination. Because RT distributions are right-skewed, the median falls below the mean and the IQR-based variance below the variance, so the robust statistics carry an offset in absolute drift and bound that the mixture moments do not. Hard cutoffs are not needed before either method; the one place a lower cutoff is needed is before *trial-level* fitting, for a reason Part II explains. Absolute parameter values are in any case not comparable across estimation procedures: the drift estimates below sit below those @wagenmakers2008lexical obtained from the same data with a $\chi^2$ fit to quantile-averaged group data of a DDM with across-trial variability in drift, starting point, and non-decision time. What travels between studies are condition effects and individual differences.

# Part I: The EZ-Diffusion Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model is the fastest of the three approaches by orders of magnitude, and within `bmm` it is no longer the standalone calculator of @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion. Recast as a likelihood over the three summary statistics of each cell [@chavez2025ez], it is a full Bayesian hierarchical model, with population-level effects, predictor structures via `bmf()`, random effects on any parameter, and shrinkage across participants. That addresses the two historical criticisms of the EZ approach, its sensitivity to contaminants, handled by the mixture preprocessing of the previous section, and its lack of a hierarchical structure [@ratcliff2008ez; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez], and it keeps the speed: every fit in this part took seconds to minutes. Tutorial 1 fits the three-parameter version to the accuracy-coded lexical decision data, tests condition effects on drift and bound, and sharpens the stimulus contrast in a refit that costs a minute. Tutorial 2 switches to response coding and the four-parameter version to estimate the relative starting point. A recovery study with a biased starting point then shows what the four-parameter version buys and what fixing $\zeta_r$ at 0.5 costs, and closes with the timing contrast that motivates Part II.

## Tutorial 1: Exploring Condition Effects with the EZ-Diffusion Model

We start with the simplest and fastest approach, the EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm`). Because it fits in seconds, it is the natural first step for exploring condition effects. The question is: *Do speed–accuracy emphasis and stimulus category selectively influence different parameters?* The formula below builds selective influence in, emphasis on bound and stimulus category on drift, so the test asks whether the effects appear where the DDM predicts them, not whether they could appear elsewhere.^[The companion script `scripts/11_tutorial1_ezdm_3par.R` contains the full executable code for this tutorial.]

### Model Specification

Specifying a model in `bmm` involves two objects: a model object that defines the measurement model and maps data columns to its components, and a formula object that gives each parameter its predictors. `ezdm()` creates the model object:

```{r}
#| label: t1-model
#| eval: true
model_acc <- ezdm(
  mean_rt  = "mean_rt",
  var_rt   = "var_rt",
  n_upper  = "n_upper",
  n_trials = "n_trials",
  version  = "3par"
)
```

The formula, written with `bmf()`, puts stimulus category on drift and emphasis condition on bound. Random slopes let each participant's parameters vary by condition: `(0 + stim_cat | id)` estimates participant-specific drift for words and nonwords, `(0 + condition | id)` participant-specific bounds under speed and accuracy emphasis. The `0 +` suppresses the intercept, so the model estimates one coefficient per factor level, separate drifts for words and nonwords and separate bounds for the two emphasis conditions, rather than an intercept plus a difference; this makes the `fixef()` output below directly interpretable.

Each parameter has a *link function* that maps the linear predictor onto the parameter scale. Drift can take any real value and uses an identity link, so its coefficients are on the drift scale. Bound and ndt must be positive and use a log link, so their coefficients are on the log scale and have to be exponentiated, as the Model Evaluation section shows.

```{r}
#| label: t1-formula
#| eval: true
formula_acc <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

Tutorial 1 uses `bmm`'s default priors. `default_prior()` lists them for any combination of formula, data, and model, one prior per row, with `dpar` naming the model parameter and `class` separating population-level coefficients (`b`) from random-effect standard deviations (`sd`) and correlations (`cor`); `scripts/11_tutorial1_ezdm_3par.R` (section 1) prints the output.

```{r}
#| label: t1-default-prior
default_prior(formula_acc, data_acc_ezdm, model_acc)
```

Two rows deserve a comment. The row for `s` fixes the diffusion noise at 1 (a constant 0 on the log scale), and the priors on `bound` and `ndt` are stated on the log scale: a `normal(0, 0.5)` prior on `bound` covers roughly 0.4 to 2.7 on the natural scale, not −1 to 1. Any prior can be overridden with `brms::prior()` and passed to `bmm()` through its `prior` argument (Practical Guidelines). If you depart from the defaults, check what data they imply before you look at your own: `bmm(..., sample_prior = "only")` samples from the prior alone, and `pp_check()` on the result shows the RT distributions your priors generate [@schad2021principled].

### Model Fitting

`bmm()` wraps `brms::brm()` with the model-specific likelihood. `sample_prior = "yes"` stores prior samples, which the Savage-Dickey tests below require; `file` caches the fitted model, so re-running the script does not re-fit it; `threads` splits each chain's likelihood evaluation across two cores; and `control` tunes Stan's sampler, with `adapt_delta` setting how cautiously it steps and `max_treedepth` capping how far one step travels. The values below are safe defaults for DDM fits, and every later fit reuses them.

```{r}
#| label: t1-fit
fit_acc_ezdm <- bmm(
  formula = formula_acc,
  data    = data_acc_ezdm,
  model   = model_acc,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  threads = threading(2),
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc")
)
```

Collected in a list, the sampler settings can be passed to `bmm()` through `do.call()`, so that each later call names only what changes:

```{r}
#| label: t1-sampler
sampler <- list(
  chains = 5, cores = 5, threads = threading(2), warmup = 1000, iter = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr", sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12)
)
```

Fitting took `r t1_time` with five parallel chains. Check convergence before interpreting anything: $\hat{R}$ should be below 1.01 and the effective sample size (ESS) at least 400 for every parameter, and `summary(fit_acc_ezdm)` shows both. Here the maximum $\hat{R}$ was `r round(t1_rhat, 3)` and the minimum bulk ESS `r round(t1_ess)`. Stan also reports divergent transitions, which `summary()` prints as a warning and `nuts_params()` counts; none of the fits in this tutorial produced any.^[If convergence issues arise, increase the number of iterations, raise `adapt_delta` (e.g., to 0.95 or 0.99), or simplify the random-effects structure; see Common Issues and Troubleshooting.]

### Model Evaluation

Before interpreting estimates, check whether the fitted model reproduces the data. For the EZ-Diffusion Model the data are three summary statistics per design cell, and `pp_check()` checks each of them: `pp_check_vars()` lists the observables a fitted model offers, and `resp_var` selects one or all of them.

```{r}
#| label: t1-ppcheck-code
pp_check_vars(fit_acc_ezdm)
pp_check(fit_acc_ezdm, resp_var = "all", ndraws = 50)
```

@fig-t1-ppcheck compares, for each statistic, its distribution across the `r lex_cells` cells in the observed data (dark) with the distributions in 50 posterior draws (light). Per-cell agreement is easier to count than to read off a density, so we also compare each cell with its own 90% predictive interval (`pp_check(type = "intervals")`); a model that reproduced the cells would leave about one cell in ten outside. Here `r t1_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]]` of the `r lex_cells` cells fall outside for mean RT, `r t1_ppc_out[["var_rt"]]` for the RT variance, and `r t1_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]]` for the proportion correct. With hundreds of trials per cell the intervals are narrow, so the check is sensitive: it shows where the cell statistics depart from what the formula allows, with one ndt per participant, one drift per stimulus category, and one bound per emphasis condition. Because the model is fit to three statistics per cell, its checks cannot show misfit in the shape of the RT distribution; the trial-level approaches of Part II can.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior Predictive Checks for the Three-Parameter EZ-Diffusion Model"
#| apa-note: "Fit to the accuracy-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data, one panel per summary statistic: mean RT, RT variance, and proportion correct. Each panel shows how one statistic is distributed across the participant × emphasis × stimulus-category cells: the observed distribution (dark) against 50 posterior draws (light), as a density overlay for mean RT and RT variance and as binned bars for the proportion correct."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "11_pp_check.pdf"))
```

`fixef()` returns the population-level estimates:

```{r}
#| label: t1-params
#| eval: true
fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)
```

The two `drift_` rows are on the drift scale. The `bound_` and `ndt_` rows are on the log scale and mean nothing until exponentiated; `Q2.5` and `Q97.5` are the limits of the 95% credible interval and transform the same way, so exponentiate the limits rather than building an interval around the exponentiated mean. This is the step to repeat for every log-link parameter in every model below:

```{r}
#| label: t1-params-transform
#| eval: true
exp(fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)[c("bound_conditionspeed", "bound_conditionaccuracy",
                          "ndt_Intercept"), c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")])
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-params
#| fig-cap: "EZ-Diffusion Parameter Estimates From the Accuracy-Coded Analysis"
#| apa-note: "Top: drift by stimulus category. Bottom: bound by emphasis condition. Each panel shows the posterior density of the population-level estimate with its mean (point) and 66% and 95% credible intervals (thick and thin bars)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "11_param_estimates.pdf"))
```

The emphasis manipulation shows the expected effect on bound (@fig-t1-params): speed emphasis produced a lower bound ($\alpha$ = `r t1_bound_speed`) than accuracy emphasis ($\alpha$ = `r t1_bound_acc`). A comparison of mean RTs could not have told whether speed-emphasis participants were faster because they processed evidence more efficiently or because they required less evidence; the model can. Drift is nominally higher for words ($\delta$ = `r t1_drift_word`) than for nonwords ($\delta$ = `r t1_drift_nonword`), but the difference is small, because collapsing all words into one category averages over high-, low-, and very-low-frequency items that differ strongly in drift, as the refit at the end of this tutorial shows. Non-decision time was $\tau$ = `r t1_ndt` s; this absolute value is specific to the estimation approach, and Part III shows how far the trial-level approaches sit from it.

### Hypothesis Testing

Because the model was fitted with `sample_prior = "yes"`, `brms::hypothesis()` can test condition effects with Savage-Dickey density ratios. Writing a hypothesis as an equality (`drift_word = drift_nonword`) asks how much the data changed our belief in *no difference*: `Evid.Ratio` compares the posterior to the prior density at a difference of zero, and its inverse is the Bayes factor (BF) *against* equality.^[With cell-means coding (`0 + condition`), no prior is placed on the difference itself; the prior `hypothesis()` uses for it is implied by the two level priors (their convolution, with $\sqrt{2}$ times the level SD) and is centred at zero here because all levels share `bmm`'s default. The `bmm` hypothesis-testing vignette and @frischkorn2026m3 [Supplement 1] give the arithmetic.] A BF of 10 means the data are ten times more likely under a model in which the two parameters differ than under one in which they are equal. As a rough guide, BFs above 3 indicate moderate evidence, above 10 strong evidence, and above 100 decisive evidence [@kass1995bayes]; all BFs in this tutorial follow this convention. Several hypotheses can be passed at once as a character vector:

```{r}
#| label: t1-hypothesis
# The seed makes the test reproducible: hypothesis() re-permutes the stored
# prior draws to build the implied prior on the tested difference
hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, c(
  drift = "drift_stim_catword = drift_stim_catnonword",
  bound = "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed"
), seed = 2026)
```

```{r}
#| label: t1-hypothesis-output
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
t1_hyp
```

For `bound`, `Evid.Ratio` is far below 1, so the evidence against equality is decisive (BF `r bf_fmt(t1_bf_bound)`): speed–accuracy emphasis changes response caution. Because `hypothesis()` estimates the two densities at zero from the draws, very large ratios are imprecise with 5,000 posterior draws [@oberauerReliabilityBiasComputational2026], and we report them only as BF $\geq$ 10,000. The `seed` argument makes a test reproducible; without it the ratio changes slightly from call to call, because the prior for a difference is built by re-permuting the stored prior draws.

For `drift` the test comes out the other way. The BF against equality is `r round(t1_bf_drift, 2)`, so the data favor *no difference* between words and nonwords by about `r round(1 / t1_bf_drift)` to 1. The estimates are not contradicted, words do show nominally higher drift, but the collapsed word/nonword contrast is too coarse to separate drift reliably. Two lessons generalize beyond this dataset: Bayes factors can quantify evidence *for* the absence of a difference, which a significance test cannot, and a selective influence test is only as sharp as the stimulus contrast you specify.

### Refining the Contrast: Word Frequency

With the EZ-Diffusion Model a sharper test is cheap. @wagenmakers2008lexical distinguished three word frequencies (high, low, very low) alongside nonwords, and the `freq` column created in the Data Preparation section carries that four-level factor. Recomputing the summary statistics per frequency level, from the same contaminant-filtered trials as the first fit, and substituting `freq` for `stim_cat` in the drift formula is the entire change (`scripts/15_cross_model_comparison.R`, section 1.1, contains both steps):

```{r}
#| label: t1-freq
data_acc_ezdm_freq <- data_accuracy_clean |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "3par",
                       method = "mixture", distribution = "exgaussian"),
    .by = c(id, condition, freq)
  )
formula_acc_freq <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

The refit took `r t1f_time` and converged (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t1f_rhat, 3)`). The equality test on the two ends of the frequency scale settles the question the collapsed contrast could not:

```{r}
#| label: t1-freq-hypothesis
# A named hypothesis prints its name in place of the formula
hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm_freq,
           c(high_vs_very_low = "drift_freqhigh = drift_freqvery_low"),
           seed = 2026)
```

```{r}
#| label: t1-freq-hypothesis-output
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
# Printed as a data frame with the columns the text reads, so the table fits
# the page width; Evid.Ratio at full precision
print(t1f_hyp$hypothesis[, c("Hypothesis", "Estimate", "Est.Error",
                             "CI.Lower", "CI.Upper", "Evid.Ratio")],
      digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The evidence against equal drift for high- and very-low-frequency words is `r bf_label(t1f_bf_drift)` (BF `r bf_fmt(t1f_bf_drift)`). Drift does vary with stimulus quality; the null result above was a property of the contrast, not of the parameter. The rank order is `r t1f_drift_order` (HF, LF, VLF: high-, low-, and very-low-frequency words; NW: nonwords), and Part III compares it with the full DDM's. The posterior predictive check of the refit leaves `r t1f_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]]`, `r t1f_ppc_out[["var_rt"]]`, and `r t1f_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]]` of the `r lex_cells_freq` cells (17 participants × 2 emphasis conditions × 4 frequency levels) outside their 90% intervals for mean RT, RT variance, and proportion correct; Part III returns to what this misfit does and does not threaten. Refining a contrast costs a minute with this model, which is what makes exploring the predictor structure with the EZ-Diffusion Model a habit worth forming before committing to a trial-level fit.

## Tutorial 2: Estimating Response Bias with the EZ-Diffusion Model (4par)

Tutorial 1 used accuracy coding, where "upper" means correct regardless of stimulus. To ask whether participants are biased toward saying "word", a question that arises in lexical decision, where word frequency creates an expectation, and in recognition memory, where participants adopt liberal or conservative criteria, you need *response coding*, where "upper" always means a "word" response, and the four-parameter version of the model, which adds the relative starting point $\zeta_r$. The companion script is `scripts/12_tutorial2_ezdm_4par.R`.

### Model Specification

Response coding changes the question from "how quickly does evidence accumulate toward the *correct* answer?" to "how quickly does it accumulate toward *word*?", so drift is positive for words and negative for nonwords. Bound and ndt keep their interpretations. The new parameter $\zeta_r$ lies above 0.5 when participants lean toward "word" before the evidence is in, an *a priori response bias* the accuracy-coded model cannot detect.

The four-parameter version needs the RT moments separately for each boundary, because that is where the starting point leaves its trace: with an unbiased start, responses at the two boundaries have the same mean and variance, whereas a start closer to one boundary makes responses there faster and less variable. `version = "4par"` of `ezdm_summary_stats()` returns `mean_rt_upper`, `var_rt_upper`, `mean_rt_lower`, and `var_rt_lower`; we use the robust statistics for the reason given under Trial-Count Constraint below:

```{r}
#| label: t2-data
data_resp_ezdm <- data_response_clean |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "4par", method = "robust"),
    .by = c(id, condition, stim_cat)
  )
```

The model object pairs the column names, and the formula adds one line for `zr`, with emphasis condition as its predictor to ask whether participants shift their starting point under speed instructions:

```{r}
#| label: t2-model
model_resp <- ezdm(
  mean_rt  = c("mean_rt_upper", "mean_rt_lower"),
  var_rt   = c("var_rt_upper", "var_rt_lower"),
  n_upper  = "n_upper",
  n_trials = "n_trials",
  version  = "4par"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: t2-formula
formula_resp_ezdm <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

### Model Fitting

Fitting uses the Tutorial 1 call with the response-coded statistics, the 4par model object, and the `sampler` list:

```{r}
#| label: t2-fit
fit_resp_ezdm <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_resp_ezdm, data = data_resp_ezdm, model = model_resp,
  file = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp")), sampler))
```

### Model Evaluation

Convergence was adequate (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t2_rhat, 3)`).
