The posterior predictive checks (@fig-t2-ppcheck) follow Tutorial 1, now with mean RT and RT variance separately for "word" and "nonword" responses and the proportion of "word" responses. Between `r min(t2_ppc_out)` and `r max(t2_ppc_out)` of the `r t2_cells` cells fall outside their 90% intervals, depending on the statistic, so the four-parameter version leaves systematic misfit in the cell statistics as well.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior Predictive Checks for the Four-Parameter EZ-Diffusion Model"
#| apa-note: "Fit to the response-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data. Panels show mean RT and RT variance for word and nonword responses, and the proportion of word responses. Each panel shows how one statistic is distributed across the design cells: the observed distribution (dark) against 50 posterior draws (light), as a density overlay for the RT statistics and as binned bars for the proportion of word responses."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "12_pp_check.pdf"))
```

Drift reverses by stimulus category, as response coding implies: $\delta$ = `r t2_drift_word` for words and `r t2_drift_nonword` for nonwords. The $\zeta_r$ estimates, back-transformed with `plogis()` from the logit scale on which `fixef()` reports them, show a small shift: $\zeta_r$ = `r t2_zr_acc_ci` under accuracy emphasis and `r t2_zr_speed_ci` under speed emphasis (@fig-t2-params). @wagenmakers2008lexical reported 0.497 and 0.476. Our accuracy-emphasis interval lies above 0.5 where the published value sits just below it, but both analyses place the starting point within 0.03 of 0.5, a very small a priori bias.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-params
#| fig-cap: "Four-Parameter EZ-Diffusion Estimates From the Response-Coded Analysis"
#| apa-note: "Top: drift by stimulus category, positive for word stimuli and negative for nonword stimuli (evidence toward the word boundary). Bottom: relative starting point by emphasis condition; the dashed line marks 0.5, an unbiased starting point. Each panel shows the posterior density of the population-level estimate with its mean (point) and 66% and 95% credible intervals (thick and thin bars)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "12_resp_params.pdf"))
```

### Hypothesis Testing

The Bayes factors against zero drift for words (BF `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_drift_word)`) and for nonwords (BF `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_drift_nw)`), and against equal bound across emphasis conditions (BF `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_bound)`), are all decisive: the selective influence pattern survives the change of coding.

The four-parameter version also makes the starting point itself testable, which is what decides between the three- and four-parameter versions on a given dataset. The point hypothesis `zr_conditionaccuracy = 0` on the logit scale is $\zeta_r$ = 0.5. The Bayes factor against it is BF `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_zr_acc)` under accuracy emphasis and BF `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_zr_speed)` under speed emphasis, where values below 1 favor an unbiased starting point. The accuracy-emphasis interval excludes 0.5 while its Bayes factor stays anecdotal because the two answer different questions: the interval says where the posterior mass sits, the Bayes factor says how much the posterior density at $\zeta_r$ = 0.5 has moved relative to the prior's, and a shift this small moves it little. This is a nested comparison, a point restriction on one parameter of one fitted model, and the Savage-Dickey ratio is the tool for it; comparing specifications that differ in more than that needs other tools (Practical Guidelines).

### Trial-Count Constraint

The `ezdm` 4par version needs enough trials on *both* boundaries in every cell. Nonword stimuli under accuracy emphasis yield few "word" responses, median `r t2_minority_median` per cell and minimum `r t2_minority_min`, too few for a reliable variance. `ezdm_summary_stats()` returns `NA` moments for a boundary with fewer than `min_trials` responses (10 by default), and `bmm` keeps such a cell, letting that boundary enter through its response counts alone, so it still speaks to accuracy but says nothing about the shape of the minority-boundary RT distribution; `r t2_cells_counts_only` of the `r t2_cells` cells entered that way. Dropping them instead would remove the cells with the most extreme accuracy. The same sparseness is why the 4par statistics use `method = "robust"`: the mixture EM cannot converge on a boundary with a handful of observations. The constraint arises whenever a condition is easy enough that participants rarely err, and no preprocessing recovers per-cell moments that do not exist. Trial-level approaches never form per-cell statistics and sidestep it; Part II returns to them. Before that, the next section asks what the lexical decision data cannot answer, because their starting point sits so close to 0.5: what does the four-parameter version buy when the starting point is biased?

## Recovering a Biased Starting Point

The three-parameter model fixes $\zeta_r$ at 0.5, and the lexical decision data barely test that assumption. Many designs do: unequal stimulus proportions, payoff manipulations, and prior expectations shift the starting point, and a model that fixes it absorbs the shift elsewhere. To see what the four-parameter version buys under such conditions, and what fixing $\zeta_r$ costs, I simulated data with a known, biased starting point and fitted both versions alongside the full DDM (`scripts/22_bias_recovery.R`).

### Design

Fifty simulated participants completed a two-choice task with two stimulus types and two bias conditions (data columns `stimulus` and `bias`), `r bias_trials_per_cell` trials per cell. Stimulus type sets the sign of drift, positive for stimulus A and negative for stimulus B, so that with response coding (upper = an "A" response) both boundaries are reached often; the bias condition sets $\zeta_r$ at 0.60 (toward the "A" boundary) or 0.40. Bound (1.5) and non-decision time (0.3 s) did not vary. Participant-level parameters were drawn around the population values with between-participant standard deviations of 0.25 (drift), 0.15 (log bound), 0.03 s (ndt), and 0.20 (logit $\zeta_r$); the drift spread is smaller than in the supplementary recovery study so that every cell keeps enough minority-boundary responses for the boundary-specific moments. I fitted the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model with a bias-condition effect on $\zeta_r$, the three-parameter model to the same cells with $\zeta_r$ fixed at 0.5, and the full DDM with the four-parameter formula, with 4,000 iterations per chain instead of the 2,000 used elsewhere, because the population-level bound mixed too slowly at 2,000:

```{r}
#| label: bias-formula
formula_bias <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stimulus + (0 + stimulus | id),
  bound ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + bias + (0 + bias | id)
)
```

### Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-bias-recovery
#| fig-cap: "Group-Level Recovery With a Biased Starting Point"
#| apa-note: "Points are posterior means with 95% credible intervals for the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model, the three-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model (starting point fixed at 0.5), and the full DDM; dashed lines mark the generating values. Panels show drift by stimulus type, bound, non-decision time, and the relative starting point by bias condition."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "22_bias_recovery_group.pdf"))
```

@fig-bias-recovery shows the group-level estimates against the generating values. All three fits met the convergence criteria of the Practical Guidelines (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r bias_rhat_max`, minimum bulk ESS = `r bias_ess_min` over all population- and participant-level parameters). The four-parameter model estimated $\zeta_r$ = `r bias_zr_A` under the A-bias condition and `r bias_zr_B` under the B-bias condition, against generating values of 0.60 and 0.40; the full DDM estimated `r bias_ddm_zr_A` and `r bias_ddm_zr_B`. All three fits recovered bound (generating value 1.5): `r bias_bound_4par` for the four-parameter model, `r bias_bound_3par` for the three-parameter model, and `r bias_bound_ddm` for the full DDM. The three-parameter model, which cannot represent the bias, absorbed it elsewhere. Its ndt estimate of `r bias_ndt_3par` fell below the generating 0.3 s by more than the four-parameter model (`r bias_ndt_4par`) and the full DDM (`r bias_ndt_ddm`) did, and its drift estimates (`r bias_drift_3par`) were pulled toward zero relative to the four-parameter model (`r bias_drift_4par`) and the full DDM (`r bias_drift_ddm`), against generating values of ±`r bias_drift_true`. At the subject level, recovered $\zeta_r$ correlated with the generating values at $r$ = `r bias_r_zr_min` to `r bias_r_zr_max` in both models that estimate it; drift correlated at $r$ = `r bias_r_drift_3par_min` and `r bias_r_drift_3par_max` for the three-parameter model against at least `r bias_r_drift_other_min` for the other two fits (scatter plots in the Supplementary Material).

The fits took `r bias_time_4par` (four-parameter EZ-Diffusion), `r bias_time_3par` (three-parameter), and `r bias_time_ddm` (full DDM). That contrast, at most around 2 minutes for each EZ-Diffusion fit against hours for the full DDM on the same 50 participants, is the reason Part II fits the trial-level approaches once, at a specification the EZ-Diffusion Model has already explored, rather than developing the model at trial-level cost.


# Part II: Trial-Level Estimation

## Tutorial 3: The Censored-Shifted Wald and the Full DDM at the Same Specification

Trial-level modeling preserves the shape of the RT distribution, allows trial-level predictors, and handles sparse cells through hierarchical shrinkage rather than per-cell variance estimates, at the price of a likelihood evaluated for every trial. The Censored-Shifted Wald replaces the two-boundary process with one or two single-boundary shifted Wald accumulators [@anders2016shifted; @heathcote2004fitting], and its simple version is the only trial-level fit that is substantially cheaper than the full DDM (Part III reports the timings). The full DDM evaluates the Wiener first-passage time distribution for every trial; it is the complete characterization of the process and the reference against which the other approaches are judged. This tutorial fits both, together with the competing-risks version of the Censored-Shifted Wald, at the specification Part I arrived at, four frequency levels on drift, so that Part III can compare the three approaches parameter by parameter. The companion scripts are `scripts/13_tutorial3_cswald.R` and `scripts/14_tutorial3_ddm.R`. The `bmm` workflow is unchanged: what differs from Part I is the model object (`cswald()` or `ddm()` instead of `ezdm()`) and the data, the trial-level `rt` and `response` columns, with `response` coded `"upper"` and `"lower"` as in the Data Preparation section.

### Preparing Trial-Level Data

The cleaned trial-level data are the input, with one additional requirement. Both the shifted Wald and the Wiener density are zero for any RT shorter than the non-decision time, so a trial faster than ndt has no likelihood, and the sampler responds by forcing ndt below the fastest surviving RT, with bound and drift absorbing the consequences. The mixture flags of `flag_contaminant_rts()` do not target this region, because the EM knows nothing about ndt; a lower RT cutoff does. The lexical decision data already carry one, since `censor == FALSE` applies the original study's bounds of 180 ms and 3 s, and the fastest RT in the cleaned data is `r min_rt_ms` ms. If your own data do not, apply a lower cutoff below any plausible non-decision time for your task before any trial-level fit, and leave the slow tail to the mixture flags.

One point about scale, because it silently invalidates comparisons that ignore it: DDM parameters are defined only relative to the diffusion noise, and multiplying drift, bound, and $s$ by the same factor leaves the predicted data unchanged. `bmm` and Stan fix $s = 1$, whereas older software often used $s = 0.1$, so reference values from that literature must be multiplied by 10 before comparison. All reference values quoted below are on the $s = 1$ scale.

### Model Specification

The Censored-Shifted Wald model object needs the RT column, the response column, and the version. The *simple* version treats errors as censored (Background), so it needs errors to stay rare, and @miller2018shifted put the guideline at 20%. The lexical decision data test that guideline once the four frequency levels are separated: accuracy-coded error rates run from `r err_min`% (high-frequency words under accuracy emphasis) to `r err_second`% (low-frequency words under speed emphasis) in seven of the eight emphasis × frequency cells, and reach `r err_max`% for very-low-frequency words under speed emphasis. We keep the specification for comparability with the other two approaches, and Part III reports whether the approximation's weak point, the bound, deviates more in that cell. The *competing-risks* (crisk) version models errors explicitly, carries no error-rate guideline, and estimates $\zeta_r$; we apply it to the response-coded data, where it can also handle the unbalanced boundary counts that limited the EZ-Diffusion 4par. The full DDM's model object needs only the two columns; there is no `version` argument, and $\zeta_r$ is included or omitted by whether the formula supplies a `zr` line.

```{r}
#| label: t3-models
model_simple <- cswald(rt = "rt", response = "response", version = "simple")
model_crisk  <- cswald(rt = "rt", response = "response", version = "crisk")
model_ddm    <- ddm(rt = "rt", response = "response")
```

Two formulas serve all four fits. For the accuracy-coded analysis all drifts are positive, and the rank order differs from the response-coded one: nonwords, which are easy to reject, have higher drift than very-low-frequency words, which are hard to recognize. The expected order from @wagenmakers2008lexical is HF (4.52) > LF (2.75) > NW (2.64) > VLF (1.80). The formula is the frequency refit of Tutorial 1, passed unchanged to the simple Censored-Shifted Wald and to the full DDM:

```{r}
#| label: t3-formula-acc
formula_trial_acc <- formula_acc_freq
```

For the response-coded analysis, drift is positive for words and negative for nonwords, with expected values HF (4.52) > LF (2.75) > VLF (1.80) > 0 > NW (−2.64), and a `zr` line lets $\zeta_r$ capture any bias toward "word" (reference values 0.497 under accuracy and 0.476 under speed emphasis). This formula serves the competing-risks version and the response-coded full DDM:

```{r}
#| label: t3-formula-resp
formula_trial_resp <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

### Model Fitting

The four calls differ only in formula, data, model object, and output file. All pass the `sampler` list of Tutorial 1, and every fit ran with two threads per chain, one fit at a time, so that the timings Part III reports are comparable across approaches (see the note to @tbl-model-comparison):

```{r}
#| label: t3-fit
fit_cswald_simple <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_trial_acc, data = data_accuracy_clean, model = model_simple,
  file = here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_simple")), sampler))
fit_cswald_crisk <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_trial_resp, data = data_response_clean, model = model_crisk,
  file = here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_resp")), sampler))
fit_ddm_acc <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_trial_acc, data = data_accuracy_clean, model = model_ddm,
  file = here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_acc")), sampler))
fit_ddm_resp <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_trial_resp, data = data_response_clean, model = model_ddm,
  file = here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_resp")), sampler))
```

### Model Evaluation

All four models converged (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t3_rhat_simple, 3)` for the simple Censored-Shifted Wald, `r round(t3_rhat_crisk, 3)` for the competing-risks version, and `r round(t4_rhat_acc, 3)` and `r round(t4_rhat_resp, 3)` for the accuracy- and response-coded DDM; minimum bulk ESS `r t3_ess_min` across the four fits). The posterior predictive checks (@fig-trial-ppcheck) cover the three observables of the trial-level likelihoods: the RT distribution, the response proportions, and the signed RT, which places lower-boundary responses on the negative axis and checks choices and RTs jointly. Unlike the checks in Part I, they can show misfit in the shape of the distribution.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trial-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior Predictive Checks for the Four Trial-Level Fits"
#| apa-note: "Fits to the Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data: the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (accuracy-coded), the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald (response-coded), and the full DDM under both codings. One row per fit; the columns show the response time, the response (lower = 0, upper = 1), and the signed response time (lower-boundary responses negative). Dark: observed data; light: data simulated from 50 posterior draws. For the simple Censored-Shifted Wald, the response and signed-RT panels reflect its censored likelihood, which does not generate errors at the observed rate (see text)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_pp_check_trial_level.pdf"))
```

The response panel of the first row shows what the censored likelihood of the simple version cannot reach. The observed data contain `r t3s_pp_lower[["obs"]]` lower-boundary responses, the errors; data simulated from the fitted simple model contain `r t3s_pp_lower[["pred"]]` on average, because errors enter that likelihood only as censored correct responses, and a two-boundary process run with the fitted drift and the doubled bound rarely terminates at the error boundary. That panel is not a test of fit; its RT panel is. The full DDM does generate errors, but fewer than observed (`r t4a_pp_lower[["pred"]]` against `r t4a_pp_lower[["obs"]]`), a shortfall the per-cell comparison in Part III returns to.

Extracting the estimates follows Tutorial 1 with two additions for the simple version: its drift is on the log link, and its bound is the single-boundary distance (Background), so both are exponentiated and the bound is doubled; the competing-risks $\zeta_r$ is back-transformed with `plogis()`. Section 3.3 of `scripts/13_tutorial3_cswald.R` applies these transformations. The doubling is a matter of definition, not of accuracy. On data simulated from a known diffusion process, the simple likelihood returns about half the generating separation, as the definition predicts, but the doubled estimate is not thereby an unbiased estimate of $\alpha$: collapsing two boundaries into one is precisely an assumption about the boundaries, and bound is the parameter the approximation has the weakest claim on.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trial-estimates
#| tbl-cap: "Part II Parameter Estimates"
#| apa-note: "Posterior mean [95% CrI], natural scale. Accuracy-coded rows compare the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (bound doubled to the full-boundary scale, drift exponentiated from the log link) with the accuracy-coded full DDM; the $\\zeta_r$ rows compare the competing-risks version with the response-coded full DDM."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
.g <- function(fe, row, f = identity, d = 2, m = 1)
  fmt_est(f(fe[row, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) * m, d)
.lv <- c(high = "HF", low = "LF", very_low = "VLF", nonword = "NW")
trial_tab <- tibble::tibble(
  Parameter = c(paste0("Drift ($\\delta$), ", .lv), "Bound ($\\alpha$), speed",
                "Bound ($\\alpha$), accuracy", "ndt ($\\tau$, s)",
                "$\\zeta_r$, speed", "$\\zeta_r$, accuracy"),
  `Censored-Shifted Wald` = c(
    purrr::map_chr(names(.lv), \(l) .g(fe_t3s, paste0("drift_freq", l), exp)),
    .g(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionspeed", exp, m = 2), .g(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionaccuracy", exp, m = 2),
    .g(fe_t3s, "ndt_Intercept", exp, 3),
    .g(fe_t3c, "zr_conditionspeed", plogis, 3), .g(fe_t3c, "zr_conditionaccuracy", plogis, 3)),
  `Full DDM` = c(
    purrr::map_chr(names(.lv), \(l) .g(fe_t4a, paste0("drift_freq", l))),
    .g(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionspeed", exp), .g(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionaccuracy", exp),
    .g(fe_t4a, "ndt_Intercept", exp, 3),
    .g(fe_t4r, "zr_conditionspeed", plogis, 3), .g(fe_t4r, "zr_conditionaccuracy", plogis, 3))
)
knitr::kable(trial_tab, align = "lcc")
```

@tbl-trial-estimates collects the population-level estimates of the four fits (`scripts/13_tutorial3_cswald.R`, section 3.4, plots the posteriors). Both trial-level approaches recover the drift sign reversal seen in the EZ-Diffusion 4par, and the competing-risks version handled the sparse minority-boundary cells that forced the 4par onto the robust aggregation method without complaint: because it evaluates a likelihood per trial rather than moments per cell, a cell with one "word" response is simply a cell with one observation.

### Hypothesis Testing

As in Part I, we quantify the evidence with equality tests. The Bayes factor against equal bound across emphasis conditions is `r bf_label(t4_bf_bound)` for the full DDM (BF `r bf_fmt(t4_bf_bound)`) and `r bf_label(t3_bf_bound)` for the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (BF `r bf_fmt(t3_bf_bound)`), reproducing the conclusion Part I reached in seconds. The full DDM's Bayes factor against equal drift for high- and very-low-frequency words is `r bf_label(t4_bf_drift)` (BF `r bf_fmt(t4_bf_drift)`), the verdict the EZ-Diffusion refit of Tutorial 1 returned in a minute.

# Part III: Comparison and Practical Guidelines

## Cross-Approach Comparison

Having applied all three approaches to the same dataset at the same specification, we can ask whether the EZ-Diffusion Model reaches the full DDM's conclusions and where the approximations diverge. "The same conclusions" means, for every condition effect, the same sign, the same rank order of the levels, and the same evidence category of the Bayes factor against equality [anecdotal, moderate, strong, or decisive; @kass1995bayes]. Absolute parameter values are not part of the criterion; the comparison reports them, and they differ. Two limits of the evidence belong at the outset. The effects tested in all three approaches are large, with Bayes factors beyond the resolution of the posterior sample, so no effect was small enough for the approaches to disagree; and non-decision time carried no predictor in any fit, so agreement was never evaluated for it. The comparison therefore illustrates the case for the EZ-Diffusion Model on one dataset; it does not settle it.

### Computational Cost

The fitting times span three orders of magnitude: `r cost_ezdm_range` for the EZ-Diffusion fits, `r cost_cswald_simple` for the simple Censored-Shifted Wald, `r cost_cswald_crisk` for the competing-risks version, and `r cost_ddm_range` for the full DDM (wall-clock of the slowest of five parallel chains, two threads per chain, one fit at a time). For the accuracy-coded frequency specification the EZ-Diffusion Model was faster than the full DDM by a factor of `r cost_factor`. That factor is not a constant of the approaches: the EZ-Diffusion likelihood is evaluated once per design cell, `r lex_cells_freq` times here, the trial-level likelihoods once per trial, `r format(nrow(data_accuracy_clean), big.mark = ",")` times, so the saving grows with the number of trials per cell and shrinks with the number of cells. The timings also come from one machine (see the note to @tbl-model-comparison). The saving of the Censored-Shifted Wald lies in its simple version, which took `r cost_simple_share`% of the accuracy-coded full DDM's time; the competing-risks version took `r cost_crisk_share`% of the response-coded full DDM's, so it should be chosen for what it estimates, not for speed.

### Accuracy-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-acc
#| fig-cap: "Cross-Approach Comparison of Accuracy-Coded Parameter Estimates"
#| apa-note: "Estimates at the four-level frequency specification. Panels show drift by word-frequency level, bound by emphasis condition, and non-decision time for the EZ-Diffusion Model, the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (bound converted to the full-boundary scale), and the full DDM. Error bars show 95% credible intervals; X markers show the reference values of Wagenmakers et al. (2008), rescaled to s = 1."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_accuracy.pdf"))
```

@fig-comparison-acc shows the accuracy-coded estimates side by side. The three approaches agree on the substantive picture: emphasis changes bound in the same direction, drift differs strongly across word-frequency levels in the same order for the three word levels (high > low > very low), and low-frequency words and nonwords sit close together in all three, with the full DDM placing nonwords marginally above low-frequency words. Where the approaches diverge, they diverge in absolute values (@tbl-cross-model-acc). The EZ-Diffusion Model's drift estimates differ from the full DDM's by `r t4_drift_pct_mean`% on average (`r t4_drift_pct_lo`% to `r t4_drift_pct_hi`% across levels), running at or above the DDM's here, most for high-frequency words, whereas against known generating values EZ-Diffusion drift is attenuated at high values when trial-to-trial variability is present [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. For bound, once the simple Censored-Shifted Wald is put on the full-boundary scale, the approaches order themselves the same way under both emphasis conditions: the EZ-Diffusion Model lowest, `r bound_ez_deficit["accuracy"]`% and `r bound_ez_deficit["speed"]`% below the full DDM, and the simple version highest, `r bound_simple_excess["accuracy"]`% and `r bound_simple_excess["speed"]`% above it. The one cell above the 20% error guideline, very-low-frequency words under speed emphasis at `r err_max`% errors, leaves a trace in drift, which is estimated per frequency level and where the simple version exceeded the full DDM most, but not identifiably in bound, which is estimated per emphasis condition. Non-decision time was `r t4_ndt_ez` s (EZ-Diffusion), `r t4_ndt_ddm` s (full DDM), and `r t3s_ndt` s (simple Censored-Shifted Wald) against a published 0.408 s; the Limitations section returns to why the trial-level estimates sit lower. The EZ-Diffusion bound lies nearest the published values (1.59 and 0.84), but those come from a different estimation procedure (Which Method to Use), so the proximity says nothing about accuracy. Absolute values are not comparable across approaches; where they matter, use the full DDM.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cross-model-acc
#| tbl-cap: "Accuracy-Coded Estimates of the Parameters the Three Approaches Share"
#| apa-note: "Posterior mean [95% CrI], natural scale, for bound by emphasis condition and ndt. Bound and ndt are back-transformed from the log link. The EZ-Diffusion column is the frequency refit of Tutorial 1, so its bound differs slightly from the first fit's. Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) bound estimates are multiplied by 2 to convert them from the single-boundary scale to the full boundary separation the other two approaches report."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
.g3 <- function(fe, row, d = 2, m = 1) fmt_est(exp(fe[row, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) * m, d)
cross_tab_acc <- tibble::tibble(
  Parameter = c("Bound, speed ($\\alpha$)", "Bound, accuracy ($\\alpha$)", "ndt ($\\tau$, s)"),
  `EZ-Diffusion`    = c(.g3(fe_t4f,  "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t4f,  "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t4f,  "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `Censored-Shifted Wald (simple)` = c(.g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionspeed", m = 2), .g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionaccuracy", m = 2), .g3(fe_t3s, "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `Full DDM`        = c(.g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t4a, "ndt_Intercept", 3))
)
knitr::kable(cross_tab_acc, align = "lccc")
```

### Response-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-resp
#| fig-cap: "Cross-Approach Comparison of Response-Coded Parameter Estimates"
#| apa-note: "Left: drift by word-frequency level; all three approaches show positive drift for words and negative drift for nonwords. Middle: bound by emphasis condition. Right: relative starting point by emphasis condition; all three approaches estimate values close to 0.5. Error bars show 95% credible intervals."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_response.pdf"))
```

The response-coded comparison (@fig-comparison-resp) asks whether the approaches agree on the drift sign reversal and on the starting point. All three recover positive drift for words and negative drift for nonwords, and all three place $\zeta_r$ close to 0.5 in both emphasis conditions, consistent with the small bias of the original analysis. In bound, the competing-risks version agreed with the full DDM to within `r bound_crisk_diff`%, while the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model placed it `r bound_ez4_deficit["accuracy"]`% and `r bound_ez4_deficit["speed"]`% lower, as the three-parameter version did under accuracy coding. Part of that gap is the aggregation method: the four-parameter statistics were computed with the robust method, whose median and IQR-based variance sit below the mean and variance of a right-skewed RT distribution (Data Preprocessing). Refitting the same `r ez4f_cells` cells from mixture moments, with the EM falling back to the robust statistics for `r mix_fallback$boundaries_fallback` of the `r 2 * mix_fallback$cells` boundaries (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t2fm_rhat, 3)`), places bound `r bound_ez4mix_deficit["accuracy"]`% and `r bound_ez4mix_deficit["speed"]`% below the full DDM's. The `r bound_ez4_offset_pts["accuracy"]` and `r bound_ez4_offset_pts["speed"]` percentage points between the two fits are the aggregation method; the rest is the approach, as under accuracy coding, where the three-parameter fit used mixture moments throughout. This fit rests on sparse cells. To keep every cell at the frequency specification, `min_trials` was lowered from its default of 10 to 3, so `r ez4f_cells_counts_only` of the `r ez4f_cells` cells (17 participants × 2 emphasis conditions × 4 frequency levels) enter through their response counts alone and some estimate a boundary's variance from three responses. That is a choice made for comparability; for a primary analysis, keep the default (Practical Guidelines).

The comparison also answers what the posterior predictive checks of Part I left open. The EZ-Diffusion fits left `r t1_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]]`, `r t1_ppc_out[["var_rt"]]`, and `r t1_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]]` of `r lex_cells` cells outside their 90% intervals for mean RT, RT variance, and proportion correct, and the frequency refit `r t1f_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]]`, `r t1f_ppc_out[["var_rt"]]`, and `r t1f_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]]` of `r lex_cells_freq`. Put through the same per-cell check from the same number of posterior draws (@tbl-ppc-cells), the trial-level fits miss at least as many cells, and RT variance is where every one of them misses most: the accuracy-coded full DDM leaves `r .tp_count("Full DDM, accuracy-coded", "var_rt")` of the `r lex_cells_freq` cells outside their variance intervals, and in `r .tp_count("Full DDM, accuracy-coded", "var_rt_below")` of them the observed variance lies *below* the interval, so the fitted model predicts more variable RTs than the cells show. The misfit therefore belongs to the specification the three approaches share, one bound per emphasis condition, one ndt per participant, and no trial-to-trial variability, not to the aggregation into summary statistics, and it sits in the absolute values and in how parameters are shared across cells, not in the contrasts. A reader who needs every cell reproduced needs a richer specification, not a different estimation approach; a reader who needs condition effects has them from any of the three.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ppc-cells
#| tbl-cap: "Design Cells Outside Their 90% Posterior Predictive Interval"
#| apa-note: "Cells (of 136: participant × emphasis × frequency level) whose observed mean RT, RT variance, or proportion of upper-boundary responses falls outside its 90% posterior predictive interval, for the EZ-Diffusion frequency refit and the four trial-level fits, each from 50 posterior draws. For the simple Censored-Shifted Wald the proportion column is not a test of fit, because its censored likelihood does not generate errors (Part II)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(ppc_cells_tab, align = "lccc")
```

Taken together, the comparison supports Part I's position for this dataset. For questions about drift and about the direction of effects on bound and $\zeta_r$, the EZ-Diffusion Model is a primary analysis, not a screening step. When the absolute values of bound or $\zeta_r$, the shape of the RT distribution, or trial-level predictors are the question, the full DDM is the tool, with the simple Censored-Shifted Wald as the affordable trial-level middle ground for high-accuracy data.

## Practical Guidelines

This part delivers the fourth learning objective: deciding which approach a question needs, and reading the differences between them.

### Things to Keep in Mind

Whichever approach you use:

- RTs must be in seconds. `bmm` does not inspect or convert the RT scale, and the default priors on ndt assume seconds; divide millisecond data by 1000 before fitting.
- The response column must contain `"upper"` and `"lower"`. Accuracy coding (upper = correct) tests selective influence; response coding (upper = one specific response) reveals decision bias. They answer different questions from the same trials.
- Bound and ndt are estimated on the log scale, `zr` on the logit scale, and the drift of the simple Censored-Shifted Wald on the log scale too. Back-transform with `exp()` and `plogis()`, credible-interval limits included, before interpreting or plotting anything.
- `cswald(version = "simple")` reports bound on the single-boundary scale, half of what `ezdm`, `ddm`, and `cswald(version = "crisk")` report. Multiply by 2 before any comparison; nothing in the output signals the difference.
- `bmm` fixes the diffusion noise at $s = 1$; older software often used $s = 0.1$. Rescale published values before comparing.
- Interpret nothing before $\hat{R}$ < 1.01, bulk ESS > 400, and zero divergent transitions hold for every parameter you report; `summary()` shows all three.
- Respect the trial-count minima (@tbl-model-comparison): roughly 30 per cell for the three-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model, which needs stable variance estimates, and roughly 50 for the trial-level approaches [@lerche2017trials; @boag2025expert]. For the four-parameter version the binding quantity is trials *per boundary*, roughly 30 divided by the minority-response rate, which is about 300 trials per cell at 90% accuracy. When accuracy is high, either let sparse minority boundaries enter through their response counts alone (Tutorial 2) or estimate $\zeta_r$ with the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald.
- `min_trials` in `ezdm_summary_stats()` sets how few responses a boundary may have before it enters through its counts alone. Keep the default of 10 for a primary analysis; Part III lowered it to 3 only to keep every cell at the frequency specification, and says so.
- Preprocess with the mixture tools, not with hard cutoffs: `ezdm_summary_stats(method = "mixture")` for `ezdm`, with `method = "robust"` for four-parameter statistics with sparse minority boundaries, and `flag_contaminant_rts()` plus a lower RT cutoff below any plausible non-decision time for the trial-level approaches (Part II).
- ndt must fall below the fastest observed RT. If an ndt estimate sits suspiciously close to your minimum RT, read the Limitations section before interpreting it.

### Other Designs

The running example is a balanced within-subject design with two-level factors. The formulas carry over to other designs with two things to know. First, because `ezdm` consumes per-cell summary statistics, a predictor must be constant within a cell: factors and subject-level covariates work, whereas trial-level covariates (a continuous item property, trial number, the previous trial's response) have to be binned into cells, which is what the frequency levels of Tutorial 1 are; the trial-level approaches take such predictors directly. Second, between-subject factors enter the population-level formula like any other factor but not the participant random-effects term, since a participant has only one level of them. Two examples:

```{r}
#| label: other-designs
# A three-level within-subject factor on drift (cell-means coding keeps one
# estimate per level; hypothesis() tests any contrast between them)
bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + difficulty + (0 + difficulty | id),
  bound ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
# A within-subject manipulation crossed with a between-subject group, plus a
# subject-level covariate (standardized working memory span) on drift
bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + load:group + span + (0 + load | id),
  bound ~ 0 + group + (1 | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

Unequal trial counts across cells need no special handling in any of the three approaches. For `ezdm`, each cell's `n_trials` enters the sampling distribution of its statistics, so sparse cells are shrunk toward the group more strongly, with the four-parameter caveats of Tutorial 2; the trial-level approaches weight every trial once.

### Inference on a Fitted `bmm` Model

Every tutorial above ran the same five steps on its fit object, and they are the steps to run on your own. The reasoning behind the last two, Savage–Dickey precision, the prior implied for a difference under cell-means coding, and when a predictive criterion is the better tool, is set out in the `bmm` hypothesis-testing vignette and in @frischkorn2026m3 [Supplement 1] and is not repeated here.

1. Convergence. `summary()` shows $\hat{R}$ and ESS for every parameter and warns about divergent transitions; `nuts_params()` counts them. Interpret nothing until $\hat{R}$ < 1.01, bulk ESS > 400, and zero divergences hold for every parameter you report.
2. Predictive checks. `pp_check()` on every observable the likelihood explains, listed by `pp_check_vars()`; for `ezdm`, `type = "intervals"` compares each design cell with its own predictive interval.
3. Estimates on the natural scale. `fixef()` returns link-scale coefficients: `exp()` for bound and ndt, `plogis()` for $\zeta_r$, and `exp()` for the drift of `cswald(version = "simple")`; multiply the simple version's bound by 2.
4. Condition effects within one fit. `hypothesis(fit, "a = b", seed = 2026)` for equalities and point nulls; read `Evid.Ratio` as the Bayes factor for the hypothesis as written, and report values at or above 10,000 as such.
5. Comparing specifications that differ in predictors or in likelihood is a different question with different tools (predictive criteria, bridge sampling) and is not part of this tutorial.

### When to Use Which Approach

The choice among the three approaches (@tbl-model-comparison) follows from the question:

- EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm`): the primary analysis for condition effects on DDM parameters and for individual differences in them, and the tool for exploring designs with many conditions. Use 3par by default and 4par when a starting-point bias is plausible; whether one is present is a point test of $\zeta_r$ = 0.5 (`zr = 0` on the logit scale) that `hypothesis()` answers from a four-parameter fit (Tutorial 2).

- Censored-Shifted Wald (`cswald`): the simple version for high-accuracy data (below roughly 20% errors) when the question does not need $\zeta_r$. It is the only trial-level fit substantially cheaper than the full DDM (`r cost_cswald_simple` here), which makes iterative trial-level model development affordable, and its bound needs doubling before any comparison. On the lexical decision data its drift ran `r simple_drift_lo`% to `r simple_drift_hi`% above the full DDM's and its doubled bound `r bound_simple_excess["accuracy"]`% to `r bound_simple_excess["speed"]`% above, so take its absolute values as approximations. The competing-risks version when errors are frequent or $\zeta_r$ is of interest; it costs most of what the full DDM costs (`r cost_crisk_share`% here), so it is a choice about what to estimate, not a way to save time. Its bound matched the full DDM's to within `r bound_crisk_diff`% on the lexical data but fell `r rec_crisk_bound_pct`% below the generating value on the simulated data of the Supplementary Material, so neither version's bound is an absolute value to take at face value.

- Full DDM (`ddm`): for questions that need trial-level information, the shape of the RT distribution, trial-level predictors, cells too sparse for per-cell moments, or the absolute values of bound and ndt. Plan for fitting times of many hours (`r cost_ddm_range` here).

"Accurate estimation" means something specific here. Outside simulations the true parameter values are unknown, so what carries applied work is whether an approach detects differences between conditions or groups and orders individuals reliably [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. On the first criterion the three approaches agreed on the lexical decision data for the two large effects tested; on the second, subject-level estimates correlated highly with their generating values for all three in the supplementary recovery study. The absolute-scale differences documented above matter when estimates are compared with published values or read as measurements on an absolute scale.

For questions that need a trial-level approach, a staged workflow keeps the cost down. (1) Explore and settle the predictor structure with the EZ-Diffusion Model, as Tutorial 1 did by moving from a two-level to a four-level stimulus contrast. (2) If error rates allow, develop the trial-level predictor and random-effects structure with the simple Censored-Shifted Wald, where each iteration costs `r cost_cswald_simple` rather than `r cost_ddm_range` on data of this size. (3) Fit the final specification with the full DDM. Divergences that follow the patterns documented here, amplified EZ-Diffusion drift differences, a lower EZ-Diffusion bound, and a higher doubled bound from the simple Censored-Shifted Wald, are expected; a reversed effect or a different rank order signals a problem with the specification or the data that is worth investigating before you finalize the analysis.

### Prior Selection

All tutorials used `bmm`'s default priors, which differ between the approaches. The EZ-Diffusion Model and the full DDM place Cauchy(0, 1) on drift, Normal(0, 0.5) on bound (log link), and Normal(-1.5, 0.5) on ndt (log link). The Censored-Shifted Wald places Normal(0, 1) on drift (on the log scale in the simple version), Normal(0, 0.3) on bound and Normal(-2, 0.3) on ndt (both log link), and Normal(0, 0.3) on $\zeta_r$ in the competing-risks version (logit link). These priors are moderately informative and calibrated for typical data. Inspect them with `default_prior(formula, data, model)`, override them with `brms::prior()`, and pass the result to `bmm()` through `prior`:

```{r}
#| label: priors-custom
custom_priors <- prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b", dpar = "drift") +
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "bound")
fit_acc_custom <- do.call(bmm, c(list(
  formula = formula_acc, data = data_acc_ezdm, model = model_acc,
  prior = custom_priors), sampler))
```

Before fitting with custom priors, verify that they generate plausible RT data with a prior predictive check (`sample_prior = "only"`, then `pp_check()`), and tighten them if the predictions are implausible.

### Common Issues and Troubleshooting

Convergence problems respond to the standard `brms`/Stan remedies: raise `adapt_delta`, increase iterations, simplify the random-effects structure, or fix $\zeta_r$ at 0.5 [@burkner2017brms]. Three issues are specific to these models. The mixture EM in `ezdm_summary_stats()` and `flag_contaminant_rts()` can fail to converge in a cell; the first function then returns the robust statistics (`contaminant_prop = NA`) and the second returns `NA` probabilities, which a `filter()` on the probability drops together with the entire cell. Both warn when this happens; check for `NA` before fitting and raise `maxit` if the warning says the EM stopped at its iteration cap. If the Censored-Shifted Wald and the full DDM disagree on bound, check first that the simple version's estimates have been doubled, then treat the remaining gap as the expected deviation (Part II) rather than a fitting problem. And if the per-cell predictive check misses many cells, the first suspect is the specification, not the approach: Part III found the same misfit in the trial-level fits, which predicted more RT variance than the cells show; relax what is shared across cells, ndt by condition or bound by stimulus, before switching approach.

# Summary and Discussion

This tutorial applied three approaches for estimating DDM parameters, the EZ-Diffusion Model, the Censored-Shifted Wald, and full DDM likelihood estimation, to a classic lexical decision experiment, all within `bmm` and all through the same three-step workflow with a different model object each time. Three themes ran through it. First, preprocessing is a substantive decision rather than housekeeping: `bmm`'s mixture tools handle the contaminants that sit away from the decision process, and those that overlap it have to be prevented by design. Second, the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model is a primary analysis in its own right. On the lexical decision data, the two large condition effects we tested kept their sign, rank order, and evidence category under the full DDM, and the EZ-Diffusion Model delivered them in minutes where the trial-level approaches took hours; the absolute values of bound and ndt differed between approaches, and the recovery study showed that the four-parameter version recovers a biased starting point. This is one dataset and two effects at the Bayes-factor ceiling, so the comparison illustrates the case rather than settling it; smaller effects, effects on ndt, and participant-level agreement across approaches remain to be tested. Third, response coding determines what a model can answer: accuracy coding tests selective influence, response coding reveals decision bias, and the EZ-Diffusion 4par runs into trial-count constraints that the trial-level approaches do not share.

Two qualifications remain. Clean convergence in sparse cells reflects hierarchical shrinkage: estimates for cells with a handful of minority-boundary responses are pulled toward the group and should be read as regularized rather than data-driven. And when the question concerns the shape of the RT distribution or the absolute values of bound or ndt, the full DDM remains the appropriate choice, with the Censored-Shifted Wald as the trial-level middle ground. For condition effects and individual differences, prior simulation work reports statistical power for the EZ-Diffusion Model comparable to or higher than the full DDM's [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]; we did not re-evaluate that result, but it is consistent with what we observed.

## Limitations

Within the scope defined in the Introduction, several things were not demonstrated: between-trial variability parameters ($s_v$, $s_\zeta$, $s_\tau$), which can improve fit but create identifiability challenges [@luken2025identifiability; @boag2025expert] and are available in HDDM [@wiecki2013hddm] or a custom Stan model if needed, and formal model comparison by bridge sampling or leave-one-out cross-validation, which `brms` provides.

One omission affects how the ndt estimates should be read. Both trial-level likelihoods require ndt to fall below the fastest observed RT (Part II). When ndt in fact varies from trial to trial but is modeled as constant, its estimate is pinned to the leading edge of the RT distribution and the remaining parameters absorb the misfit [@miller2018shifted]; this is a plausible contributor to the ndt ordering in the Cross-Approach Comparison. The approaches are not equally exposed. A forthcoming `bmm` extension adds a uniform trial-to-trial ndt component (`sndt`) to the Censored-Shifted Wald likelihood. `ddm()` uses the four-parameter form of Stan's `wiener_lpdf()`; the seven-parameter form [@henrich2024seven] integrates over the variability distributions numerically and is far more expensive, with a single simulated dataset of 500 trials taking 20 to 44 minutes on average in their simulations, parallelized over 40 to 80 threads per chain. The EZ-Diffusion Model estimates ndt from the mean RT rather than from the fastest responses: with across-trial variability in ndt at the high end of empirical values, @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion [pp. 14–15] found drift nearly unbiased, bound somewhat overestimated, and ndt somewhat underestimated.

# References


# The EZ-Diffusion Likelihood in bmm {.appendix}

For an unbiased starting point, MDT and VDT are the expressions given in the Background; @grasman2009ez give them for any starting point, separately for each boundary. The sampling distribution of the mean and the variance of $n$ decision times depends on the first four cumulants of the decision-time distribution (cumulants are the moment-like quantities that add over independent components; the first two are the mean and the variance): MDT, VDT, and the third and fourth cumulants $\kappa_3$ and $\kappa_4$, which carry the skew and the tail weight. These cumulants are not computed from the observed RTs. They are the values the DDM implies for the current drift, bound, and $\zeta_r$, recomputed whenever the parameters change. @srivastava2016moments [Eq. 28, p. 101] derived the cumulant generating function of the decision time conditional on the response and from it the first three moments; `bmm` obtains $\kappa_3$ and $\kappa_4$ by differentiating that function three and four times, an extension @srivastava2016moments [p. 105] note is possible but do not carry out (see `?ezdm_dist`). With $n$ the number of trials in the cell, the likelihood is

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_{\text{upper}} &\sim \text{Binomial}\big(n, P(\text{upper})\big), \\
s^{2}_{\text{RT}} &\sim \text{Gamma}\!\left(\tfrac{\text{VDT}^{2}}{W},\; \tfrac{\text{VDT}}{W}\right), \\
\overline{\text{RT}} \mid s^{2}_{\text{RT}} &\sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\tau + \text{MDT} + \tfrac{\kappa_3 / n}{W}\,\big(s^{2}_{\text{RT}} - \text{VDT}\big),\; \sqrt{\tfrac{\text{VDT}}{n} - \tfrac{(\kappa_3 / n)^{2}}{W}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
W = \frac{\kappa_4}{n} + \frac{2\,\text{VDT}^{2}}{n - 1}
$$

is the variance of the sample variance. In words: the sample variance is Gamma-distributed around VDT with a spread that the fourth cumulant widens, and the sample mean is Normal around $\tau + \text{MDT}$, shifted by however far the observed variance sits from its expectation, because in a right-skewed distribution the two statistics are correlated. When $\kappa_3 = \kappa_4 = 0$ this reduces to independent Normal and scaled chi-square terms, the form that treats RTs as if they were normally distributed, which @chavez2025ez proposed.
